utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I start the evidence of this witness, I just remind the Court that he's available only for today. He's now a schoolmaster, and it's very difficult for him to take time off, and indeed the financial consequences of his being here fall on the school, not on the U.N., because there are no provisions for dealing with it. The second thing is, as a result of discussions had with the witness yesterday and this morning, I have reordered the summary and very slightly added to it. So I hope you've now got a different version, which is in a slightly more logical order, to help in the presentation of evidence. With this witness, I regret to say there are one or two additional documents -- not very many, just a couple -- that we must produce. Unfortunately, the relevant printer for that particular type of document is not disgorging its material at the moment, so unlike the most recent witnesses, it won't be quite as smooth in the presentation of documents as it could be. Some documents will have to be handed out as they arrive through the door. I've been helped by my learned friends indicating, in relation to the earlier version, what is not objected to and can be led, and that will enable me to save time and deal with the evidence in chief, I think, quite swiftly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please, Mr. Whitworth?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It's Mr. Lee Kent Whitworth, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Formerly a captain in the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire, presently a teacher at a school in Leeds, or Yorkshire in any event?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Arriving in Vitez early in May 1993, were you first a regimental signals officer performing the duties of establishing and maintaining the communications network?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In June 1993, were you assigned as liaison officer for the Vitez area, with the boundaries at Novi Travnik T-junction and at the south at Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's approximately correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were your functions to develop good relations with people on the ground in order to facilitate the delivery of aid transports in the Lasva Valley generally?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you assess the communication ability of both major warring factions?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As regimental signals officer, it was the sort of thing I noticed as I was doing my business around the Lasva Valley area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the ABiH was concerned, did you assess that they had access to a rechargeable type of transceiver radio with which they were able to communicate within Stari Vitez but also with the regular forces on nearby hills?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yeah. They had good internal communication with hand-held radios, and they could also reach 325 Brigade headquarters in Poculica on the hillside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it appear that they relied on generator power in order to recharge the batteries of those radios?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, in the absence of any form of resupply, which we didn't see they had, it seemed common sense that they were using a hand portable generator of some description there, one which had been seen in there previously by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you observe at a later stage that the ABiH had a PTT communication in Poculica linking them to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes. They re-established the telephone lines, and brigade commanders had a landline through to the ABiH headquarters in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn then to your overall assessment of the communication ability of the HVO. First, was there, in your judgement, any interference by any party, the HVO or anybody else, with your communications systems? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were several incidences where white noise was used to jam and block out the UNPROFOR radio communications, and it was strongly suspected that the HVO were responsible for those, as there were -- members of the HVO actually came upon the net at some point and used my Hotel 21 call sign and started mocking our use of the airwaves. So we strongly suspected that it was them that was transmitting white noise in order to disrupt our communications up and down the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Their communications within the HVO were how good or bad?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I witnessed hand-held portable radios. In the Hotel Vitez itself, there was some type of telex machine. They had PTT landlines laid connecting Busovaca to Vitez, and, in general, communications seemed pretty thorough up and down the Lasva Valley area. They also received faxed or telex-type messages from other areas out of the Lasva Valley that they didn't have direct road contact with, and that was how the likes of Colonel Blaskic, as their commander, kept himself informed. They were using possibly local satellite communications of some description.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To be specific, what communications did they have to Kiseljak and also to Kordic's Eagle's Nest retreat, as it's been described?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was a landline. There was a PTT telephone line that had been surface laid or through trees that ran all the way along the river into the Busovaca area, and there were telephones in use in the Eagle's Nest. So there was obviously a complete PTT line into Busovaca and, in all likelihood, out along the river line connecting to Vitez, which is what we had found at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any -- because it went through ABiH territory, I'm not aware of any PTT facility. But there were -- they did have radio communications in the form of telex machines of some description.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you saw one particular manifestation of communication ability strung up in central Vitez.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. HF is a commonly-used type of radio. It's not technical or difficult. It's commonly used in mountainous terrain. I saw one or two examples of what looked like HF antennas in various parts, which could quite easily have been used to transmit extremely long distances. In fact, HF will go around the globe without a lot of difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn to a different form of communication; helicopters. Can you tell me what, if anything, you observed yourself by way of helicopter movements?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was supposed to be a no-fly area in Central Bosnia, but that was regularly breached. There were HIP helicopters that landed for a brief phase on almost a weekly or daily basis in, I think it was, June or July, and they were landing in the quarry/motion area around the back of Vitez, the ammunition factory. They would spiral in very, very quickly because obviously they were in danger of being engaged by ABiH forces, land, stay for half an hour, an hour, and then disappear again. That's the type of helicopter movement in and out. I would say it took place relatively regularly over a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say "HIP helicopters." To which body did these helicopters belong, if you were able to establish that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They came in at high altitudes, so it's very difficult to discern from which direction they came. But assuming that they were landing in HVO territory, they must have -- I assume they came from Croatia. I witnessed similarly marked helicopters that landed at Kiseljak, HV helicopters that landed at Kiseljak, and similarly at Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is, I think, in the bundle of materials to be provided, although it's got to be added to, as I've indicated, at the back of it there are a collection of colour photographs and then some black and white photographs. They, I hope, all have numbers on them. There's a photograph to be produced, 2641,2. It may be helpful if the Judges have the whole bundle themselves and it will save time, and if the witness could have a bundle as well and the usher, then although things won't be quite as smooth as they have been with recent witnesses, we should save time. If it's possible for the witness to have a bundle himself and then he can do the selection himself, and the usher can put the appropriate photographs on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While you're finding the appropriate photograph, Mr. Whitworth, the position is your own notes, which might have enabled you to deal with matters in strict chronology, are no longer available to you because you provided them to someone in the military and you haven't had them back. But you did take your own photographs, a large number of them, and they do help you with recollection of detail. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Our extensive notes that were taken as liaison officers were handed over to the milin on completion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're now looking at 2641,2, and this is -- explain.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This is one of the helicopters coming in to land near the quarry area at the back of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. One other small matter of general description, paragraphs 9 and 10. Right from the beginning, did you have several meetings with the defendant Mario Cerkez, and does photograph 2516 give a general picture of the sort of meetings, negotiations, that you had? Can you identify people there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the meetings that was chaired by the ECMM early on in the tour when we were still trying to broker some form of relationship between the HVO and the ABiH, and there's Colonel Blaskic on the far right there and several of his staff officers at the table waiting for the ABiH representatives to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give any of the names of those other staff officers or not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think, if my memory serves me correctly, the chap in the grey hair on the left could be Mr. Filipovic, but my memory is not that clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Paragraph 11, and I think this is something I can lead, but I'll wait for Mr. Kovacic to confirm. It was paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: 10 in your version or in our version?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate if you will not lead the questions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, did you go to Cerkez's headquarters in the cinema, and if there, what did you see of a broadcasting facility?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I visited Commander Cerkez quite frequently, and he was usually quite a pleasant and welcoming host. On one particular occasion, he actually asked me to listen to the local radio which he had on his desk, and he banged on the wall and shouted something through to the adjacent room, and up came the latest hit record that was being broadcast on the radio. That was a very sort of stirring and nationalistically-based pop song that I assume was to rouse the local people in their determination to resist further military attacks. It was basically a bit of a rebel song probably used as a form of propaganda. I didn't understand the lyrics, but there were certain key words in there which made it quite clear that that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the output of that local radio programme generally?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It covered all the local matters happening in the Lasva Valley/Vitez area and was used as a supply -- to supply the local people with information to keep them updated on what matters were actually happening in the Vitez pocket there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I turn to the 11th of June of 1993 and to the Convoy of Joy? Was there an encounter or meeting at the Dubravica checkpoint just to the east of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was, sir, yes, involving Ambassador Thebault, one of the senior ECMM ambassadors, Colonel Alastair, and Colonel Blaskic. There had been a large convoy, I think it's about eight to ten kilometres long, that had been heading up with various forms of humanitarian aid. The convoy had been put together by the people in the north of Bosnia and had journeyed south to collect various resources and forms of aid and then was making its way back north to supply the local population. Once it got into the Lasva Valley/Vitez area, it had been stopped, interrupted, and there had been a major confrontation between the local population and the convoy itself, during which time the convoy was broken up, vehicles were disseminated and looted. Several of the drivers were killed, and the progress of the convoy was completely halted. I was involved, as the liaison officer for the area, in trying to facilitate the onward movement of the convoy, but earlier on it was similar brokering the cessation of aggressive activity towards the convoy, getting people like Colonel Alastair and Colonel Blaskic together to agree that the convoy should move onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see anything of Mario Cerkez at this event or encounter?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The day -- the convoy had been halted late one evening, and a lot of the looting had taken place that night, in the early hours the following day. We got Ambassador Thebault, Colonel Alastair and Colonel Blaskic together, and despite assurances by the HVO Croat authorities that the convoy would be allowed to move on, that wasn't the case. It was being stopped by the local population. All the vehicles had disappeared, and some of the drivers and occupants of the convoy were being held hostage. So basically what I had to do was get the commanders on the ground, along with Colonel Alastair as the senior U.N. representative, to go to the area at the Dubravica checkpoint where one of the major blockades, the blockade of the Convoy of Joy, was happening, and there was a large gathering of Croat civilians there preventing any onward movement and the reassembly of the convoy. I got Ambassador Thebault, Colonel Blaskic, and Colonel Alastair together and physically got people to break up and allow the convoy to move on its way. Mario Cerkez was in the crowd, and I could observe him what looked like to me doing his best to stay out of public view, or out of the view of Blaskic and Thebault, and watching what was going on without actually assisting or taking part, as such, himself. On that particular occasion, I remember Blaskic recognising Cerkez. Karlo Grabovac was also in the crowd of people, and we strongly suspected that it was being orchestrated at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: General Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- we have to leave a gap in interruptions to allow the interpretation to catch up. You said that -- wasn't taking part, Cerkez, and you mentioned Grabovac. Do you mean weren't taking part in the demonstration, or weren't taking part in controlling and stopping the demonstration?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In the latter. We had been given assurances by Colonel Blaskic, and I think by Dario Kordic at the time, to Colonel Alastair that the convoy would be allowed to move on uninterrupted and that it would be reassembled in order to do that. But that actually, physically, wasn't happening on the ground, which is why we had to drag Colonel Blaskic and Ambassador Thebault and Colonel Alastair out in front of the people to say, "Look, this shouldn't be happening."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then, as you were about to tell us, Blaskic did something in relation to Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He did. He spotted him in the crowd and called him out, and it was obvious that commander Cerkez didn't want to come out. He then -- when commander Cerkez was addressed by Blaskic, it was done so in a very reprimanding way, and it looked to me that he was being reprimanded, to say, "These are your local people, your local soldiers. I've issued my orders. Let's get on with it and let this thing move on out of the area." I think Blaskic was losing face in front of Ambassador Thebault and Colonel Alastair, so there was a certain amount of disagreement, or so it appeared to me at the time, between what Cerkez wanted to happen and what Blaskic had given orders to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you form a view as to what part, if any, Cerkez may have had in the original detention of the vehicles, or their retention?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My impression was that -- certainly that there had been an orchestration of the civilian people. They had no real way of knowing what was going on at the far end of the Lasva Valley other than that which was broadcast on the radio or passed deliberately by word of mouth. It just seemed at the time that these large gatherings of crowds and this resistance to the convoy moving on, despite the fact that it contained both Croat and Muslim people, moving through the Lasva Valley to the north, it just seemed that it had been orchestrated by the local senior dignitaries in the area, i.e., both military and political.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that if we now turn to Exhibit 1044, which is a milinfosum dated the 11th of June, do you have that document? It can be looked at in two parts. First, did you contribute directly to this milinfosum, and in particular, which paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. It was my job during the night and during the day to go around and identify where people and vehicles actually were that had been separated from the convoy, so there are several references in here to mines being laid, people being held, vehicles disappearing. Those were contributed by the likes of myself and other --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 refers to a chronological account which one can find -- and I'm not going to go through it in detail -- at the back of this five-page document, the last two pages being a summary of events. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we come back to the first sheet of this document, paragraph 3, was that a passage that you contributed?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would just like to read that out.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It makes reference to the dissension towards Colonel Blaskic, and Dario Kordic being cited as the only respectable authority in the Lasva Valley area. And this is typical of the comments that were directed at times towards Colonel Blaskic. I think he was seen, as far as certainly the people in Vitez were concerned, as an ineffective military commander, although, to his credit, he had quite an area of responsibility, and the overall military command of the Vitez area fell locally to commander Cerkez. It was our opinion at the time, because of how quickly things had happened and the nature of what had happened, that it had been orchestrated and coordinated. Vehicles had been ferried off to various quarters. There had been HVO troops involved in the stopping of the convoy and in the shooting of some of the drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other points about paragraph 3. Answer them briefly, if you will. Karlo, who was he, what's his reference? And secondly -- I'm going to ask you both questions at once because of the delay that we have to have between question and answer otherwise -- secondly, the conclusion that it was Dario Kordic who had orchestrated the attacks. Comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: "Carlo" is Karlo Grabovac; he was one of the battalion commanders under the command of Mario Cerkez, so he was quite an influential figure locally in Vitez, and I had several dealings with him throughout my time in the Vitez area. Kordic was seen as the key political and executive decision-maker in the Lasva Valley pocket, whilst the military commanders, obviously, were the executors of the political will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the conclusion that was expressed there, was that your conclusion at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The comment, you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was my and several of the other liaison officers' opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn then to the probable next event, something that happened on the 11th and the 12th of June involving some U.N. armoured vehicles. I think I'm allowed to lead on that. So far as that's concerned, was there an incident on the 11th and 12th of June, at night, where some seven to eight U.N. armoured vehicles were taken hostage by Croat civilians; all access routes out of Vitez being mined; the ABiH started shelling the area, and a man called Darko Kraljevic, whom you met, threatened to kill you; you then went to the Hotel Vitez, where you found ECMM monitors who had been brought there, apparently, for their own safety; you were successful, by negotiation with men called Gelic and Grabovac, to arrange the release of the United Nations vehicles and of the ECMM observers. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The perception at the time of this incident, by you and perhaps your fellow soldiers, was what?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That this was another orchestrated move on behalf of the HVO to draw attention to their -- partially to the plight of the Croat population in Vitez. Also, it was relatively early on in our tour; it was assessed to be possibly an exercise by the HVO in testing our resolve, to see what methods we were going to use in comparison to our predecessors, who experienced very different circumstances. So it was again -- it again looked very much like it had been contrived and orchestrated by the military commanders on the ground, and it was the likes of Karlo Grabovac and Colonel Blaskic who I negotiated with at the time for the release. But it did seem, on reflection, that it was more locally orchestrated than at Colonel Blaskic's level. He gave assurances that it wasn't happening and it wouldn't happen, but it took a lot of pressure in negotiation on the local battalion commander, Karlo Grabovac, and again with Darko Kraljevic, who appeared to be the senior HVO authority responsible for the surrounding and mining of the vehicles in the centre on the particular night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will return to Kraljevic shortly, but meanwhile, two points upon which I would like your succinct assessment. First, Cerkez's approach to and respect for Blaskic's orders; and second, the relations between Blaskic and Cerkez generally.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic never appeared to be held in particularly high regard by commander Cerkez, and there were occasions when commander Cerkez was demeaning of Colonel Blaskic's authority, position, and effectiveness as a military commander. To be fair to commander Cerkez, he was engaged in more local matters, i.e., the defence of the Vitez pocket, as opposed to Blaskic, who had wider, more strategic concerns. So it was easy to see how maybe a local commander could perceive his high commander's ineffectiveness. But there were times when commander Cerkez was condescending towards the efforts and authority of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Their relations generally, co-operation between them?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was a reluctant co-operation between them. I think I saw Cerkez only once visit the Hotel Vitez, and there were occasions when Blaskic's authority was -- or instructions and orders were ignored by commander Cerkez and his subordinate commanders, i.e., the likes of Karlo Grabovac, for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any coincidence of co-operation and the movement of the troops of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My experiences were that commander Cerkez was very familiar and had a good relationship and rapport with the commander of the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic. Kraljevic was cited as one of the 3rd Op Zone effective fighting units, and under the command of Colonel Blaskic, such units were used by the HVO and deployed up and down the Lasva Valley pocket to execute offensive action in their defence of the area. I know that commander Cerkez and Kraljevic worked together on several military actions that took place on the south of Vitez and spoke of each other in high regard, particularly of Mario Cerkez towards Kraljevic. I think Mario saw Kraljevic as a very, very useful asset, military asset, that allowed him to undertake and complete his mission with great success.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the Vitezovi were being deployed, what, if anything, did you notice of co-operation between Cerkez and Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Other than being familiar with the fact that the Vitezovi were part of the military units under Colonel Blaskic's overall command, nothing immediately springs to mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: -- of them being delegated to commander Cerkez's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I think it's your position that Blaskic was the overall military commander in respect of both brigades and military police in the Lasva Valley area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that the local commanders were more interested in defensive matters in their own areas of operation but were obliged to follow Blaskic's orders?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Albeit reluctantly at times, yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the Exhibit 1087 be turned up, please. It's the milinfosum for the 20th of June. Does this document, Mr. Whitworth, include and contain an assessment of Blaskic's position?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It does so, yeah, part 10B --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the second sheet.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: -- lists the organisations that Blaskic cited as -- on the official paperwork that he released -- as under his command, and included in that is the 4th Military Police Battalion, the Vitezovi, and Tvrtko 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that the Chamber will be assisted if you just run through, very swiftly, the titles for which letters -- initials are given, in (i) to (vi), Roman.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: (i) and (ii), I have to be honest, escape me. I think one of them is an artillery stroke indirect fire weapon unit, rocket launchers, that type of thing. (iii), (iv), and (v) are -- (iii) is 4th Military Police Battalion that was co-located in Hotel Vitez; (iv) is the Vitezovi, the Vitez Knights, commanded by Kraljevic; and (v) is the Tvrtko 2nd Battalion, which is, from my experience, based more towards the Travnik end of the Lasva pocket; and Zuti was a local criminal, black marketeer, who was also quite influential in the area, was known to have his finger in all sorts of different pies, from wheeling and dealing cigarettes, vehicles, drugs, weapons, and was quite a key influential figure in the Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last sheet of this document sets out in table form those conclusions, does it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. This was the result of several weeks of liaison work. We actually managed to put together an OrBat, an order of battle, what we thought -- where we thought people fitted in to the overall structure of the HVO based in the Lasva pocket, with commander Blaskic the overall 3rd Op Zone commander. There were two or three other HVO brigades in the Lasva pocket, one of which was Busovaca, one of which was Vitez, and there had been previously one in Travnik, before the fall of Travnik. As the Vitez LO, I managed to get all the information together there on the personalities involved in the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. Paragraph 17, and I think almost the last paragraph that I'm not going to lead, apart from concluding paragraphs. Was there a high-level meeting in Kiseljak which you think occurred probably in June?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. We were asked by the U.N. headquarters in Kiseljak to provide transport and facilitate the occurrence of one of their high-level meetings between the ABiH and the HVO that they were going to chair in Kiseljak. So we provided armoured vehicle protection from Vitez for all the local senior political and military dignitaries in Vitez through ABiH territory into Kiseljak for the meeting to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And they travelled there by prior arrangement, in Warriors, through ABiH territory?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn to the photographs that you took, starting at 2507, perhaps you can tell us or inform us -- or remind us, rather -- of the names of people insofar as you can now recall them.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The three gentlemen in military uniform, front right, with the sunglasses on, is Anto Valenta leaving with his briefcase and no intention of coming back. The gentleman to his left, his name escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then there is Mr. Kordic behind that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Behind that is Mr. Kordic, behind him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this part of the gathering of the local dignitaries before you loaded them in the Warriors and took them into Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah. Mr. Valenta was a very key political figure at the time, and Mr. Kordic was seen as his representative on his departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So 2508, I think it's simply more of the same, without any additional names for you to give us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The names escape me, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 2509: This is, is it, with the Hotel Vitez itself in the background on the right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's taken in central Vitez, sir; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the pointer, to avoid any ambiguity, if you would just point out names that you can identify, names of people you can identify.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Blaskic [indicates], Dario Kordic [indicating]. There's the gentleman, again, whose name escapes me [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Up at the back, by the corner of the building?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This gentleman here [indicates], I'm reasonably confident that is Darko Kraljevic, but it's not a very clear photo. I didn't actually know him at the time, but retrospectively now, it could well have been him. He was of that build and -- and of look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were photographing these people from the back of a truck or something like that, were you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back of a vehicle. Next photograph, 2510, still, I think, more of the same, still at Vitez; yes. A couple more names here I think you may be able to help us with. The man in the yellow shirt?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's Mr. Skopljak. He was the local political representative, i.e., based in Vitez. The gentleman in the blue T-shirt is mayor Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we can just go on to Photograph 2511. Does that relate to this event, or to another event?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir. That's General Petkovic visiting Nova Bila hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I thought so. It's my mistake; I've put it in the wrong place in the summary. So withdraw that photograph for the time being, and we'll go back to the events of the trip to Kiseljak. Having gathered these people up, did you take them to Kiseljak for their meeting?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you offer them return facilities in order to get back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was arranged by U.N. headquarters in Kiseljak, yes, that we would go back at a specified time and date and return to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, did they all come back in the Warriors?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, they didn't. If I remember correctly, there was about seven or eight people who didn't return short of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Including?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Mr. Valenta, Colonel Blaskic. I think -- I'm quite sure Dario Kordic didn't come back as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You brought these people then back through enemy lines to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see, in Vitez, those who had not availed themselves of the offer of a lift?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: At a later date, sir, yes, I did, and met with Mr. Kordic in Busovaca at a later time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, had they been provided with any safe transport from British Battalion or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, they hadn't, sir. They must have really gained access into the pocket by some other means, as the Lasva pocket was obviously surrounded by ABiH troops and they hadn't been provided by transport at a later date, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So by what means, in your judgement, may they have returned?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was strongly suspected at the time that people like Colonel Blaskic could have been using the HIP helicopters to move in and out of the area, and there was no reason to suspect why key senior dignitaries like Kordic didn't have access to similar types of transport to be able to move south to Croatia and back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Meetings of the kind that had been organised at Kiseljak, did they become less effective after a while, with the consequence that British Battalion liaison officers dealt at a different level of authority?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes. Kiseljak became more and more ineffective. The commanders in the Lasva pocket, along with their ABiH counterparts, were less and less interested in brokering any sort of relationship with a view to ceasefires, et cetera, and so it became a more locally-agreed thing. The likes of myself and the other liaison officers were involved in brokering local ceasefires or prisoner exchanges or casualty evacuations. It was all done through us, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 18. Did you meet Valenta at Blaskic's headquarters, where Valenta had an office which was covered with maps outlining Croat areas in the country and population charts showing ethnic composition, Valenta himself being clear in his objective that Croat areas should be cleansed of Muslims, he suggesting that this was something that would happen in the near future and was something over which he had influence?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes. As far as Valenta was concerned, he had two or three maps on the wall with pie charts showing the pre-population breakdown and said that as far as he was concerned, what was happening in the Lasva Valley was inevitable and would result in it becoming a Croat enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Santic, who we've seen on the photograph, mayor of Vitez, was somebody you met and who appeared to have good relations with Valenta, Cerkez and Skopljak, although I think you assessed that Cerkez eventually played a role of different significance, is that right, in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A greater or smaller role than Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A more significant role, a greater role, really, in Vitez. As things became more and more desperate after the fall of Travnik and the HVO being forced into an ever-decreasing area, the ABiH to the south of Vitez and to the north put a lot of pressure. There was several military actions which put the Vitez Brigade under a lot of pressure, and obviously their commander likewise. So I think he became a more important and influential figure as far as the Croat people were concerned and under a lot more pressure as a consequence of all the action that was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 20 you've dealt with substantially already. A couple of supplementary points on Cerkez being in company with Kraljevic and appearing close with him. Was he often or not in company with Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think I only actually physically saw them in each other's company on one or two occasions, but on several occasions when I went to visit Commander Cerkez towards the end of the tour, his staff officers in the cinema would cite him as being in the Donja Vecerska area, looking at the military situation there. Then I would attempt to visit Kraljevic, and his own troops would say he's working with Mario and he's up country with a view to whatever military activity they were planning at the time. So rather than seeing them on several occasions, although I did witness them on one or two, they were referred to by their own troops as being together on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cerkez appearing to have overall responsibility for what extent of Vitez and its surroundings?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Commander Cerkez was responsible for the defence of the Vitez pocket. He was a local man and held in high regard by the local population, and he was responsible for the command of all the militia troops on the ground that were defending the pocket against ABiH military activity and, as any commander would be, undertaking whatever action to re-establish their military position on the ground, and that included the use of offensive action and the use of the likes of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your assessment, did his responsibility extend to Donja Vecerska or areas like that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, that was part of his brigade areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 21. The Vitezovi were well equipped with automatic weapons and uniforms, Kraljevic himself being feared, you would have judged, but revered by the HVO and Croat population, he having taken over the headquarters in Donja Vecerska sometime in the middle or end of 1993. The ABiH held him responsible for many of the early HVO offensive actions, and indeed Kraljevic once boasted that he had mined an HVO complex itself in Donja Vecerska when the HVO were withdrawing from the area and the ABiH were moving in, the explosion killing soldiers and demolishing a substantial part of a hillside; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Just to explain, sir, yes, the complex was actually a trench complex which was high on the hill initially occupied by the HVO. The BiH were trying to assault from the south into Vitez on that particular direction. Basically, what happened was the HVO troops withdrew from the trench positions that had been mined by Kraljevic and his troops. As the HVO withdrew, the ABiH occupied the trench positions. Then they blew the trenches up, and they claimed losses of between two and three hundred ABiH troops on that particular occasion. Kraljevic provided us with a film showing the explosion, and he was quite proud of his handiwork on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Alas that film, which was shown in Blaskic, has not yet surfaced, so I'm not in a position to play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 22. Do you recall two incidents involving Cerkez and the exchange of prisoners and Muslim refugees? I've reordered them from the earlier version so that they are probably chronological, although the text hasn't been appropriately amended. Was there one involving some 20 to 30 Muslim refugees who wanted to go to Zenica and were detained by the HVO close to the front lines, and did you approach Cerkez about this?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to Pero Skopljak about it and to Mario Cerkez about it at the time. There were 20 to 30 family groups -- 20 to 30 people, rather, as family groups located in some humble accommodation near, I think it was the Rijeka area, a couple of hundred metres from the front line. They were actually DPs, displaced persons, that had moved into the Lasva Valley area sometime earlier. That was information relayed to me by Pero Skopljak at the time. I said to Mr. Skopljak that it wasn't really in their interests to be accommodated so close to the front line, and he said that they were staying there because they didn't want to facilitate the removal of more Muslims from the areas than had already taken place. I said to him that it would be in everybody's interests if they were seen to be released and allowed out of the area as a gesture of goodwill by the HVO/Croat population in Vitez. They didn't want to stop there. They wanted to go to Zenica, where they had relatives. He agreed with that. Then I tried to -- I spoke to Mario Cerkez about it, and he said, no, that they had to stay where they were. Eventually, I went up and -- as the U.N., we weren't allowed to put them in vehicles and move them, so I walked with them. I said, "If you're as free to move as I'm told you are, then you can walk out of here," and walked with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was despite Cerkez's reluctance or resistance?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. We were stopped by military police and local HVO militia as we left, and they got quite aggressive and waved guns around and said they weren't going anywhere, they had to move back to where they were being accommodated. I went to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we must cut this short, but eventually they had to go back, and you only discovered that they were released three months later?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct. Well, they disappeared when I went back some time later. I had heard they had been somehow or other moved to Zenica, although I never confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the other exchange you think in the period of July to August of 1993; two civilians taken out by the Red Cross from Stari Vitez for medical treatment, kept temporarily in Cerkez's basement headquarters, his attitude, and again deal with it as briefly as you can. It's his attitude to this that we're interested in, being what?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We were rather incensed by the fact that he had stopped the ICRC and removed two chronically-ill people as they were being casevaced to Zenica. He was adamant that they weren't going anywhere and he wasn't going to allow what he called the free movement of people in and around the area because organisations like the ICRC were obviously providing weapons and ammunition to the ABiH pocket in Stari Vitez. He did get quite aggressive about it, and we eventually went into a conversation that involved if I could release troops that had been captured by the ABiH in the Kruscica area, that we could come to an agreement and he would subsequently release the two people being held by the HVO in Vitez. I visited them both. They were both kept in a cell, so -- I'm not quite sure whether it was actually in the cinema. It was in a building in the centre of Vitez -- one of whom who was chronically ill with something like TB or something like that. We went on to do an exchange later on of three young boys that had been captured by the ABiH for the two prisoners, and that nearly didn't take place because Mario Cerkez said that he wanted, as well as the three boys in exchange, he wanted three members of the special forces that I assessed to be the Vitezovi at a later date that had been captured in some military action earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. That was resolved how?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Eventually, I managed to bring the three boys back into Vitez, the three Croat boys, and the two members of the -- the two chronically-ill Muslims were released into the possession of one of our liaison officers and taken to Zenica for their medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I turn on, I realise I overlooked just producing three photographs for a quick consideration in relation to paragraph 21, the Vitezovi. If you would be good enough to turn up, please, the photograph of the sniper rifle, 2641,8, and then later in the pack, the two photographs, 277,3 and 277,4. Very swiftly, just comments on those three as they relate to the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's one of the American sniper rifles, 12,5-millimetre long-range sniper rifles. They are an expensive and rare weapon. That type of weapon was one we suspected had been involved in the death of Boris, the UNHCR driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To which we'll be coming in a minute.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That happened earlier on in the year. These photographs, the ones I took, that's the Vitezovi headquarters in Donja Vecerska and members of the Vitezovi brandishing this particular firearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph. Comment?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's one of the Vitezovi soldiers comparing weapon sights on one of our weapons with the one they were in possession of, the American sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Likewise, 277,4, the next photograph, again the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The gentleman in British military garb that stood in the middle is the intelligence officer, so I periodically took him out to introduce him to personalities, and he confirmed the calibre of weapon with the weapons and the theories I had originally come up with. He was an expert on weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well, then. Let's, in the summary, go to paragraph 23, which I can lead, and it's photograph 277,5 that we may look at. Was there a group you judged an extremist group called the Jokeri, with whom you had several contacts, they been located in an alpine-like hut near Nadioci, shown in photograph 277,5?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. I think I met them twice there and then they disappeared. That was what we call the Swiss cottage or the alpine hut in the Nadioci area. That's Captain Mark Bower, another fellow liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, it's photograph 2775. I cited it incorrectly. The Jokeri were mostly young men wearing black, heavily armed, some 30 to 40 in number being based at this alpine hut, and some of them boasting to you that they were the spearheads of any HVO attack, claiming it to be an elite group of military police with a history of successful military operations in the Lasva Valley. Their commander was the commander of the HVO military police, Pasko -- the name isn't said there, but it's Ljubicic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At the time, they didn't betray to me his surname. They just said he was called Pasko. On subsequent investigation, I tied Pasko Ljubicic in to the Jokeri.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: HOS, to your knowledge, were based in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. As a unit, I don't recall ever seeing them. I saw several individuals throughout the tour bearing HOS insignia and saw one or two badges worn by troops that were involved in the Grbavica feature. But as a unit, I never saw them intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not that numerous. You saw them as an adjunct to the HVO troops, their typical dress being high-tech Magnum boots and clean wind-cheater-style jackets, and you saw some of them in the attack on Nova Bila, which we'll deal with a little bit later?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to the Stari Vitez problem, Sefkija Dzidic was the ABiH commander there. Your judgement was that Stari Vitez was fairly well equipped with weapons and ammunition, although there was no official ABiH headquarters there, and you judged, I think, that the HVO in a sense used Stari Vitez as a bargaining chip whenever the BiH from Zenica was behaving in a strong or too-strong a way. What you mean by that, rather than me putting it into your mouth, can you just explain that in a sentence?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In the absence of the BiH pocket in Stara Bila, there would have been nothing, really, to stop the ABiH mounting major military campaigns and assaults onto the Vitez area and shelling it heavily with mortar, artillery fire, et cetera, et cetera. With the communications between Stara Bila -- sorry, Stari Vitez and 325 Brigade, if there was any major military activity going on, then there were direct communications between the two, and there was one occasion where Sefkija actually called for a cessation of ABiH activity on the north side in 325 Brigade because they were coming under increasing pressure themselves in Stari Vitez. So it was quite easy for HVO to apply pressure to ABiH forces throughout the Muslim pocket in response to any ABiH activity elsewhere in the Lasva Valley and for Commander Sefkija to bleat about it up the chain of command to 3rd Corps and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having communications with the commander of 325 Mountain Brigade on the hills above Vitez, any sniping or the throwing of improvised mortar bombs was immediately communicated to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're going to see a little bit more what these improvised mortar bombs were able to do and what they amounted to in a couple of minutes, but to conclude what I want you to help us with about Stari Vitez, is it right that on one occasion an armoured vehicle carrying what was thought by British Battalion to be bandages and medical supplies to Stari Vitez, in fact had ammunition wrapped within it, and that was discovered and led to a problem?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did. We worked very hard at having good relations with both the HVO/Croats and the ABiH/Muslims, and there was a constant accusation by the HVO that we were substantiating the Muslim positions in Stari Vitez by supplying them with weapons and ammunition. Obviously, this wasn't in our mandate, and we went out of our way to try and prevent this type of thing happening. We had a liaison officer in the UNHCR building and the ICRC to make sure things were monitored what were happening in Zenica. On one particular occasion when I brought some medical supplies in, and this was quite early on in the tour, I had a habit of wandering around and just assessing the situation in Stari Vitez and came across them unpacking the medical supplies, and within each of the cartons of 20 -- sorry. Within each carton of bandages was wrapped a package of 7,62-millimetre rounds. To be fair, there wasn't actually that much small-arms ammunition in the package that we had taken in, but nevertheless if that was a trickle feed on a regular basis, it could amount to quite a large amount. On discovering this, I had a considerable sense-of-humour failure with Commander Sefkija. I told him that he betrayed my trust and left, and I told him that I would no longer supervise and facilitate the movement of medical supplies or food in unless it had been personally checked by myself, because he jeopardised my relationship with the HVO and the Croats to his own ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 1147,1 is a milinfosum for the 19th of July which I want in respect of only one small passage. Is the Vitez contribution on the first page of this exhibit something contributed to by you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, that was contributed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This deals with a conversation you had with Sefkija Dzidic, the commander, it says there -- this is under paragraph 3 -- of Stara Bila town defence, not Stari Vitez. But can you deal with what is said in subparagraph B in particular about the claim for HV involvement?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He -- actually, the information included here was relayed to myself by the likes of Sefkija, and he was adamant that at least troops dressed in Croat military garb, as he recognised as HV, had been involved in the assault, and one of our suspicions at the time was that if not equipment then possibly men at times could have been moving into the area by the use of helicopters that we had identified previously. So it wasn't an unreasonable assumption on his part, although it remained unconfirmed. We had no way of confirming that they were actually Croat forces as opposed to local HVO militia involved. They could quite easily have been just in complete HV uniforms, but he was adamant of the fact that they were HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see that the comment in respect to this particular attack says that, "Whether they will attack," that is, whether the HVO will attack, "Stari Vitez again is difficult to assess after an initial failure," and then goes on to conclude, in the assessment of those preparing the report, there must have been some stockpiles of weapons?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: If I may, sir, there was the ammunition factory, and one of our suppositions was that it was high-tech devices that were being brought in by the HIP helicopters. General munitions, in theory, could have been manufactured in the ammunition factory in Vitez, but things of a technical nature like the percussion caps to artillery shells, for example, couldn't be manufactured there, and so those typically were the things we suspected as being brought in by helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not entirely in chronological order but to be dealt with at some stage are the two killings in respect of which you became specifically involved. Was there first the killing of a UNHCR driver who had been attempting to get an armoured vehicle into Stari Vitez; had a sniper round been fired from a position a considerable distance away, and did the sniper round go through the vehicle, the flack jacket, and kill the driver, you being in a position to examine the impact point and the vehicle; the HVO denied any involvement, saying that they had no access to such kind of weapons which were, indeed, rare; that this is the type of weapon that you've shown us on the photograph as being available to Kraljevic, and the photograph, if we've got it, 433/18, as it was called -- I think it might be in black and white only -- it's Z2015. Forget the earlier number. It's in black and white. Thank you very much. Interpret this for us, please.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's a picture of the 12,7-millimetre round embedded in the bulletproof glass at the front of the vehicle. It had entered from the right-hand passenger side, gone through the Kevlar armour plating, then through the back of the chair and through the driver's chest and embedded itself in the front window. That's the -- 12,7 millimetre is the calibre of the American sniper rifle we saw earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The assessment of the position from where that round had been fired was made by you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was about a thousand metres away?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it's a whole kilometre. Was that an HVO position?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was indeed, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we must have been talking too fast. We must give the interpreters time to catch up. The second killing was that on the 5th of July of a BritBat interpreter called Dobrila, the killing being close to the BritBat base itself and being by a 7,62 round, fired from what distance and from whose position?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was fired from approximately 100, 150 metres away, from the HVO side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us what -- again, in short order -- what happened so far as the HVO position and investigation is concerned.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Just background to the shooting, first of all. There was the captains and Dobrila, or some of the interpreters, occupied one of the houses on the ABiH/Muslim side of the road. On exactly the opposite side of the road, 10 metres away, were HVO/Croat-occupied houses. We even stood out on the balcony one night and a small-arms exchange had broken out, as often happened in the evening. We'd taken cover inside of the building, heard Dobrila cry out, and she had been shot through the head by one of several rounds that had hit the side of the building. I was asked by the colonel to investigate it, and when I studied the path of the round, it had quite obviously -- from where Dobrila had been situated, it had quite obviously come from the HVO side. Colonel Blaskic knew Dobrila and was himself -- appeared upset by the shooting of a U.N. interpreter, and he commissioned a group that came from the Vitez Brigade, if I remember correctly, who were responsible for investigating it with a view to punishing those responsible, which was the assurance given by Colonel Blaskic at the time. The conclusions of the two, three-day investigation that I led with the HVO was that an ABiH soldier must have gained access to the HVO positions during the firefight, sniped the round at Dobrila, and then gone back onto their own territory. They refused to acknowledge that it would have been a HVO or Croat soldier responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say that's the conclusion of the investigation that you led, was that your conclusion or the conclusion of others?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was the conclusion of the HVO investigative team. My conclusion was that it had been shot -- we identified the firing point; it was the top, as you look at it, left-hand window, from one of the houses regularly occupied in HVO territory by HVO snipers, and it had come from that particular window.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you think it was realistic and possible that an ABiH would have infiltrated that position, sniped, and then crossed back to his own territory?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not within the realms of possibility under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn to Nova Bila and an attack on that location: Was that a running problem?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nova Bila, the attack on it: Was it a running problem?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was a problem that got worse as far as the HVO and the Croat population were concerned. The HVO and BiH lines were in very close proximity, with the camp sitting in between, and the BiH had a hillside, i.e., the Grbavica feature, from which they would snipe over the top of the BritBat camp into the Croat and HVO positions on a nightly basis, and of course the HVO would return fire. So the HVO were at a considerable tactical disadvantage and were incurring considerable casualties as a result of this sniping exchange that regularly took place. It did get considerably worse towards the end, until at one particular occasion, Mario Cerkez said to me that it was going to get sorted out, that they had had enough of it, they had taken enough casualties. I, personally, as the LO, had tried to appeal to the BiH local commander to cease the sniping activity, told him that he was going to lose a lot of goodwill from the UNPROFOR camp, as he was jeopardising the safety of our soldiers as well. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Slow down. Was the attack one which included the use of anti-aircraft guns positioned by the HVO near the BritBat camp?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was about 800 metres away, yes, on the high ground facing Grbavica feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Cerkez tell you that Nakic was involved?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of the staff officer he named at the time. I went down there and complemented him and massaged his ego as to how successful a military operation it had been, as the assumption by me was that the Vitez Brigade had been heavily involved in it. He said yes, it was a good attack, and that he hadn't been -- but he hadn't been responsible for the staff work and planning of it, although he had obviously been involved in it to a certain degree. The troops that were identified on the day were from various units, i.e., had been brought in specifically for the operation, but included Vitez Brigade troops and troops from further down towards the Travnik end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the one particular group that was identified as being involved another elite fighting force?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: At the time, I thought I identified gentlemen who might be seen as part of the Vitezovi, involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about Tvrtko?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were people wearing Tvrtko insignia on the jackets, and there were people wearing local HVO militia badges as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm now in a position to distribute the documents that weren't available earlier, in packs for everyone. Just four documents to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you've got the first document, which is Z1175, the milinfosum for the 20th of August, under "Vitez," is this your contribution to the milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that deal with a matter we've already touched upon, over halfway down the "Vitez" entry, Cerkez threatening to resolve the Grbavica problem in the near future?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think we need to dwell on that any more at the moment. If we turn to the following day, the next exhibit, 1176,1, 21st of August, does this deal with the same problem -- I'm sorry, I've temporarily lost my place. Under "Vitez," just interpret that for us, please, if that has any --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This is just citing one of the regular small-arms and sniping exchanges that took place between Stari Vitez and Central Vitez, the ABiH and HVO territories respectively, and it records the death of Boris Jozic. He was the exchange officer whom I worked with to organise body exchanges between the ABiH counterpart and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you make -- or help us a little bit with the Boris Jozic death. Was that the subject of comment at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was, yes, sir. It was commented by people on both sides that Boris was actually essentially a nice guy, which I had born witness to myself, but he wasn't particularly an enthusiastic supporter of the current regime in the centre of Vitez, and it was offered to me as an -- that he was possibly knocked off by his own troops, assassinated by his own troops, or offered up, as it were, because of his lack of empathy with the current situation in Vitez. That was unsubstantiated, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I've very nearly -- well, as you can see, I've only got a few paragraphs to go, but it will take us 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 33. You have already summarised the attack on Grbavica, I think you viewed as a legitimate military target; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: However, after the attack, was there destruction of civilian houses and looting?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There appeared to be systematic destruction of the property after the attack had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you take the colour photographs, we can deal with what they show of this quite quickly. The first photograph yet to be looked at doesn't relate specifically to Grbavica. It's 2039, and it depicts a photograph of the "baby" bombs held by --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it's Mirad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Held by?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it's a chap called Mirad, who is one of the local commanders in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Rebisic; is that the name?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It could be. I just knew him as Mirad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is an example of the bomb, the "baby" bombs, the home-made bombs, is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we pass on in this stack of photographs to 2641,9, and then we just quickly go through those and the following photographs --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't think I have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To save time, simply, take mine. The first photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, that's a picture I took on leaving Vitez, looking towards the Grbavica feature, as I was returning to the BritBat base.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it shows?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It shows a large number of buildings burning, and that's during the daytime of the Grbavica assault by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph, this, I think, shows up to those looking at the photograph directly better than on the ELMO, and in one version of this photograph you can even see the point of firing of a "baby" bomb. Can you point out what should be visible and may be visible on original copies?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The assaulting HVO troops were using the rear of the house as a launch point for the "babies" that were being launched from here, and there is a better photograph showing the flash, and the bombs were then tumbled straight over the building and land two or three hundred metres further forward where they'd explode when the fuse burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this photograph, you've actually captured the "baby" bomb in midair; have you not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It shows up as a small point above the house. The next photograph, please. This is where?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This is within the houses of Grbavica. These are troops immediately after the assault, if not while the assault is taking place, further up the Grbavica feature. These are just troops going through the area doing a bit of looting, by the looks of things. These are HVO troops responsible for the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can see the radio in the left hand of the left-hand man.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The chap has got a big chopper, butchers knife, of some description.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's the same Grbavica village, and burning. You can see all the buildings are being gutted by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next, please? The same again?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, the same again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subsequent? Keep going on, please. Another house being burned?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. Again, these are all photographs I took at the time. This was as I was driving through Grbavica on my return from the Hotel Vitez and my conversations with Darko Gelic about the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph, please. More burning. And again. Now we see what about the house on the right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Those are the two houses we saw originally. They were the original launch point for the infantry attack, and they now have the Croat flag flying on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Those are some of the troops involved in the assault, one of whom I knew personally, who is difficult to make out on that. It was part of the Tvrtko Brigade battalion structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Some of them wore military police insignia. They were wearing -- some of them didn't wear any insignia or badge at all, and that's Supa or one of their girl friends in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If I could have those photographs back, please. Did you discuss this event with Cerkez and did he say who had planned it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He said that he hadn't been responsible for the staff work in planning. The name escapes me. It may have been Filipovic or Nakic who had been involved in the actual staff work and planning of the actual exercise, but there were Vitez brigade troops involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The two milinfosums that deal with this are, respectively, numbers 1198,1 and 1201,1. Do you have those? As to the 9th of September, 1198,1 under "Vitez," is that your entry?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is, sir, yes. I did not personally witness the decapitated body. That was -- we sent an armoured vehicle into the village because it wasn't particularly safe immediately after the battle, in case of any reprisals from the ABiH, so we sent an armoured vehicle in to go have a scavenge around and see what the situation was inside. It was they that identified a dead ABiH soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Decapitated and disembowelled?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As stated there, the other -- this was tied in with a report from the Dutch transport battalion who had witnessed -- who were based towards Busovaca, who had witnessed this decapitated head being passed around, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think perhaps we can just look at the next exhibit, 1201,1, milinfosum for the 14th of September. I think that's the one. In any case, the one for the 14th of September under Vitez, is that your entry?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You deal there with what Darko Gelic had said, that the HVO troops involved in the recent fighting to capture Grbavica had come from the 2nd Battalion Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. That was the battalion based around the Grbavica -- just further west of the Grbavica feature, and I think the battalion commanders name was actually on the order of battle that we looked over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You declined to comment on the suggestion that troops may have come from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As stated there, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then gave the reasons to negate the constant sniping, reasons for the attack?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Correct, which had been offered to me similarly by Commander Cerkez earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can obtain by this afternoon, but for some reason it hasn't yet surfaced, there was a milinfosum dated the 15th of September, 1993, dealing with an ultimatum about Stari Vitez. Do you recall that? If not, I'll have to seek leave to put it in later.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I have recollection that there was an ultimatum given at some point, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Made by --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it was Commander Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll, with leave, produce what I hope before Mr. Kovacic starts his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I ask your other conclusions, can we just look at the few remaining photographs to explain things? We'll take the stack of photographs, passing beyond those that dealt with the departure of the people for Kiseljak. We then come to 22511, which is the first of a couple of photographs showing Petkovic and Blaskic. Just explain that, if you will. These are a miscellany of points. Again to save time, I just hand mine in quickly. Have a look at that. Don't worry about going through your stack. I'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's General Petkovic, who was one of the senior Croatian military commanders at the time based, I think, in the Mostar area. He had been brought up to Kiseljak and then been brought in by ourselves in armoured vehicles along with the U.N. representatives. He had come up to negotiate with us regular helicopter flights in and out of the area, with a view to using them for casualty evacuations.
