We discussed this with Colonel Alastair, the liaison officers and myself, and decided that it would open us up to all sorts of accusations from the ABiH if we allowed this to go ahead, and so Colonel Alastair told me to attend the meeting and prevent the helicopter flights from coming in, so I was sent along to negotiate with General Petkovic. Colonel Blaskic met him as the senior HVO commander on the ground. We visited the Nova Bila hospital, which is where that photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph, please, and that really tells that story?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. The Nova Bila hospital was unfortunately the only medical facility that the Croats had in the Lasva pocket, and as you can see there, a bed was made up of two hospital -- sorry, two church benches pushed together, and the crypt was used as an operating theatre. It was quite something, really. We didn't allow the helicopter flights in, but what we did do is I organised regular road evacuations to Kiseljak, where later, helicopter flights were allowed out off to Croatia with the injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could I have those photographs back, please. Thank you. Then there are a few more. Can you take that one, and have you got these two?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These are just for personalities who we may need to identify -- well, one is of you, and the others are personalities. Thank you. First the view.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's looking north from HVO trench positions. That's not in the Vitez Brigade area; that's further toward the Travnik end. I can't remember the name of the place, but those are HVO trench positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Next photograph, please. This is 2778. Yes, who's that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's Pasko Ljubicic, commander of the military police, and he was overseeing the inspection and searching of a UNHCR convoy that was going partly to Kruscica, partly to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's -- the gentleman to the far left, with the military uniform on, is Darko Gelic, liaison officer to Colonel Blaskic. Two gentlemen are local civilian police, because they operated the checkpoint where the vehicle was stopped. And the gentleman centre, or right-hand side, in the military uniform, is Pasko Ljubicic, and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: -- the same incident. Liaison between military police and Colonel Blaskic's liaison officer, which is the function of Darko Gelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last photograph of this type?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's the -- that's Karlo Grabovac, battalion commander, one of the Vitez Brigade battalion commanders, stood on the road out to Kruscica. You can see a mine bottom right there; that's a sniper screen, and that's when I was trying to organise a body exchange and aid delivery to Kruscica and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is only for personalities, so that we can know who people are if it becomes necessary. Then there are four black-and-white photographs, and that's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, this one relates, I think, to Stari Vitez, does it not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, that's -- initially, when we arrived, we had access along the main road into Vitez, i.e., we could get into Stari Vitez from both sides. Quickly this vehicle was erected with TNT on the side, and mines were placed across, so we only had access through HVO-controlled territory; we didn't have access straight into Stari Vitez, so the HVO could control access of ICRC, UNHCR vehicles, myself, in and out of Stari Vitez a lot more effectively with that one end mined off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next photograph, which I think again relates to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. It's very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a request to slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's a photograph taken inside Stari Vitez looking out towards Vitez town centre, and those are ABiH troops on their front-line positions, and there's a concrete wall that's whited out, that you can't see, that marks the beginning of HVO territory, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This photograph and the signs above the door, the significance?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's a photograph taken on the steps of the Hotel Vitez, myself and one of my soldiers, some of the local HVO militia and police based in the hotel. The signs above the door on the left say "Op Zone Vitez," and the one on the right is "HVO Military Police." So there were -- headquarters of both were co-located in the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was a visit to the brigade commander, whose name escapes me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the man in the white shirt, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the significance of --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a moment. The significance of the brigade commander and his brigade and its location, in your judgement, being ...?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That it was pretty much co-located with Mr. Kraljevic's -- sorry, Dario Kordic's Eagle's Nest. That was the brigade headquarters. I can't remember if it was in the same building; if it wasn't, it was very close, down the same valley feature. That's Darko Gelic, who was, again, the liaison officer of Colonel Blaskic there, who had taken me to meet the same people in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're finished with the photographs; many thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your assessment of Kordic's position in relation to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was seen as the key political and executive decision-maker in the area, the -- shall we say the understudy of Mr. Valenta, who had since left, and very influential, and in terms of the local population, he was highly regarded. Colonel Blaskic was the key military figure in the area, responsible for the overall strategic command of the Lasva Valley pocket, and further north, other HVO territories; but Dario Kordic was seen as the key -- shall we say policy-maker in the Lasva Valley pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to both Kordic and Blaskic, what was their attitude towards speaking to officers of your rank?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were pretty indifferent and saw us as insignificant. The likes of Kordic wouldn't really talk to anybody of my rank or the liaison officer based in Busovaca, but he would have audiences with Colonel Alastair, who was obviously the senior U.N. figure in the Lasva Valley area and quite influential from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you only saw Kordic at the Hotel Vitez on the one occasion?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, and I met him maybe two or three times more than that, but not at a personal level; just simply through organising meetings between himself, maybe the ECMM, or himself and Colonel Alastair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subject to producing the milinfosum of the 15th of September a little later, if I am allowed to, that's all I ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not object to Mr. Nice posing further questions to Mr. Whitworth regarding the additional milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, or nearly afternoon, Mr. Whitworth. My name is Stephen Sayers, and along with my colleague, Mr. Naumovski, we represent Dario Kordic. I will be asking you some questions first, and then I'll be followed by counsel for Mario Cerkez, Bozidar Kovacic and Goran Mikulicic. One of the first things that I have to cover is you tend to speak quickly, as do I, and it is important to leave a gap between the question and the answer so that the interpreters can catch up. I'm confident we'll run afoul of that rule, but let's do our best to try to observe it. Let me ask you general questions first, sir. My understanding is that you first arrived in the Vitez area in early May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it was the middle of May, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Middle of May?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you left your area of operations in early November of the same year?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, the 7th or the 8th, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So essentially you were in Central Bosnia for five months?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It felt like a lot longer, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I believe that you have given a statement to investigators for the Prosecution initially on August the 14th, 1996, three years ago?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: (Inaudible).

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you did not sign that until about a year later, on May the 14th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You testified for two days in the Blaskic case, giving about 290 pages of testimony, from July the 13th to the 14th, 1998?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then later in the year, in October -- on October the 9th, to be precise -- you gave further testimony in the Kupreskic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I believe that you are 35 years old at this point.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm getting older, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As are we all. And therefore you were 29 years old when you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is no criticism of you, Mr. Whitworth, but apparently -- I believe that the interpreters are having trouble picking up your words, so if you could speak up a little bit, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You do not, yourself, speak Croatian, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I picked up one or two words, but no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You couldn't carry on a conversation?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you arrived in mid May of 1993, you've previously told us that you were the regimental signals officer for a while, and then, on the orders of your CO, Lieutenant-Colonel Duncan, you became the liaison officer for Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your predecessor in that position, I believe, had been then-Captain Angus Hay?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, he covered the whole of the Lasva Valley area. When we arrived, Colonel Alastair soon ascertained that it was a fundamentally important job, and so he put more people in liaison officer jobs and gave them specific areas of responsibility, geographically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Duncan, I believe, felt that the area covered by Captain Hay was basically too much for one person to handle and therefore split it into two separate areas?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the liaison officer for Busovaca was Boris Kalen?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's true, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So he handled affairs in Busovaca, and you were responsible for affairs in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The approximate geographical limits were the Busovaca T-junction to the Travnik T-junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that you were responsible for the area to the west of the T-junction, and Mr. Kalen was responsible for the area to the south of the T-junction?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. During the course of your tour, I believe you were with the 1st Battalion of the Prince of Wales Own Regiment?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have testified that you found that ceasefire agreements and checkpoint agreements became increasingly -- that's not a correct way to put it -- became decreasingly effective or increasingly ineffective as time wound on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Would you rephrase that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Happy to. You testified, I believe, that during your tour, your perception was that ceasefire agreements and checkpoint agreements became increasingly less effective, and that's why you made the decision to deal with lower-level commanders?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever agreements were broken proved to be very fragile and very locally based, and so we ended up dealing with people on a more local basis. We always dealt with people on a local basis anyway, to ensure that the passage of orders and instructions from high commanders had taken place. It was too large an assumption to assume that because Colonel Blaskic or commander Cerkez had issued an order, that it would have reached a checkpoint or something later on on the ground. So we always did that anyway, but it became more of a focus. We had to build up the rapport and relationship with local people, because they did tend at times to take things into their own hands, so we had to win their confidence as well as that of their commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think you said in your statement of three-or-so years ago that that was essentially a bottom-up approach?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: "Bottom-up" meaning that we had to cover everybody, not just the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the superior commanders in the chain of command were not particularly happy with your decision to deal directly with their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think that was the case, on one or two occasions, the likes of commander Cerkez might have reprimanded not myself, but his commanders on the ground. I was aware that he had reprimanded several commanders on the ground which I had brokered local agreements, and people had -- I had managed to talk people into allowing me through into Kruscica, for example, and that was not commander Cerkez's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The events that we have been discussing cover events that occurred over six years ago. You have testified that you kept a contemporaneous journal or diary, but that that is no longer available because it was turned over to your regiment at the end of your tour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir. We were actually issued with police notebooks, and those were the things that we kept notes in. When we finished with a notebook, they were handed in, because they were, to all intents and purposes, legal documents, and they were used for us to refer to at the end of the day, when we were discussing matters with the intelligence officer. They were also, at the end of the tour, taken back in, disposed of in whatever way, filed away, so the information didn't go out of theatre, as it were, or into the wrong hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In your statement three years ago, you told the investigators that because you had not been provided with copies of those notebooks, it was difficult for you to be able to recall a strict chronology of events. Have you had access to those notebooks in preparing for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir. I've refreshed my memory using the milinfosums, some of which I can't recall, others of which, depending on the nature of the incident, I have very clear recollections about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's perfectly understandable. The milinfosums were based in part, I believe, upon the notes that you wrote down in the police books that you were issued?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. At the end of each day, we would have a thorough debrief with the intelligence milinfo officer, so that any information that we had collected during the day could be centralised and help to build up the picture of the situation in our tactical area of responsibility. Then everybody was briefed accordingly so the colonel was fully aware of what was happening throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Have you had the opportunity to consult the milinfosums to prepare for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I've read through one or two of them, yeah, and refreshed --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All of the ones that you needed to review were made available to you, I take it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I've read through quite a number of them, some of which, as I said earlier, don't strike a chord with me, I can't recall having said those things, others of which I have vivid recollections about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We've had quite a bit of testimony from other officers regarding milinfosums, but would it be fair to say that, generally speaking, they provide a contemporaneous chronicle of any major event of significance?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, they are a document containing all the key issues, and then added to the factual information is usually a comment provided by the intelligence officer who is trained to assess and rationalise that information as to future activities or the likelihood of various things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Because they provide a contemporaneous chronicle of significant events and meetings and so forth, they are very useful to consult in order to refresh your memory, just to order your recollection chronologically of those events and meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. Actually I have very vivid recollections of certain key events, and the -- where I find fault in myself is actually at which point during the tour those things happened, or which one happened before another, as it were. So yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Whenever you consulted one of these milinfosums, I take it, Mr. Whitworth, that you took a look at the full document and not just snippets of it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Usually I just read the Vitez bit, and that was the bit that I contributed. So not the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that you testified in the Blaskic case -- and there's absolutely nothing wrong with this, but from consulting the milinfosums, they assisted you in, on occasion, working out memories which had been jumbled into a more systematic and sensible fashion and actually made you realise that some of the statements contained in your 1996 and 1997 witness statement were in fact not accurate?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't -- anything -- any -- anything that wasn't accurate, I think the only questions that arose were my initial statements I gave in 1996, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: -- where I got one of the two events jumbled, chronologically speaking; i.e., some things took place earlier or later than I had originally said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. You corrected that when you were asked the questions in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to the situation that confronted you when you arrived in Central Bosnia in May, isn't it true that, in your view, just about everyone was armed?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. It was an unusual set of circumstances, the likes of which myself and the rest of the soldiers hadn't come across before, and those people who weren't actually physically bearing arms usually had access to some arms or another, so it was difficult to differentiate at times between those who were actually regular troops, those that were militia, and the different units, because they weren't always bearing arms, as it were, but nevertheless had affiliations, maybe not just to one military unit, but maybe to others, as well as responsibilities to their own village, the defence of their own village, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also saw women bearing arms occasionally, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall an example in the Lasva Valley. The only example that springs to mind is a visit to Sarajevo, and a Serbian female soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Didn't you see women bearing arms in Stari Vitez, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Could possibly have done, as most people in Stari Vitez at some time or another took responsibility for guarding a bit of the perimeter. So that's -- I could have well commented to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you say "possibly," but you actually did see women bearing arms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, this isn't a memory game. If you've got some information that the witness said on an earlier occasion that he saw a woman with arms, just put it to him, rather than taking it round the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Mr. President. I'll do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked in the Blaskic case, at page 10.378, on July the 14th, whether men and women were active in the defence of Stari Vitez, and you said, "I saw women bearing arms as well, if they were of that ilk." I don't think it's a big point, Mr. Whitworth, but it would be fair to say that -- that's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would say that, bearing in mind they represented 50 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Did you participate in any of the meetings of the joint operations command or the Busovaca joint commission that used to meet in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: During the early part of our tour, we facilitated the occurrence of such meetings, one of which I think we organised, and I moved people around, and it took place in one of the ECMM buildings, and another one -- one of the later ones, I think -- was one of the photographs that you would have seen there, where we actually arranged for it to take place in Vitez. But that was during the very early part of the tour, and that stopped quite soon after we arrived. It's the same meeting, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that whenever incidents occurred and you spoke to representatives of the warring factions, it was absolutely routine for one side to blame the other?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely, and to exaggerate the circumstances that had actually happened. That was part of our job, to try and visually confirm and get several accounts of the same thing, and that's why the job of the intelligence officer in writing the milinfo reports was vital, because he was getting opinions from quite a few different people. We ourselves would do that, as well, on the ground, from both sides, locally speaking, and we would tend to err on the conservative side, as opposed to the exaggerations that each of the respective commanders would come up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One other general question, if I may. You found yourself basically on the front lines of a war zone. Would you agree, Mr. Whitworth, that it's a sad but factual reality that burned out houses were a regular sight in Central Bosnia throughout your tour in both Muslim and Croat villages?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that. I think I personally witnessed -- what I personally witnessed was very much based on the Lasva Valley, so I don't feel able to comment on the surrounding areas. I certainly didn't see a lot of derelict and burned-out buildings when I transited to Zenica and visited the ABiH area. But it always appeared systematic when there was any military activity taking place in the Lasva Valley area. There is no reason why buildings should set on fire when subjected to small-arms fire, and so the number of buildings that were ablaze strongly suggested to us that it had been done deliberately to remove the possibility of anybody being able to move back into the area and reinhabit those houses. It was remarkable how the Croat-occupied houses within Grbavica remained untouched during the military assault, so it did very much appear it had been done on a systematic basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We'll talk about the Grbavica incident or the operation in September of 1993 later in your cross-examination, but isn't it fair to say that one of the principal reasons for the military operation on that hill was to eliminate a sniper nest, if you like, or a sniper position that was regularly used by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct. It did appear to us to be, from that point of view, a legitimate target. I had made several appeals to local ABiH myself that they were going to get themselves into deep trouble, they were losing a lot of goodwill from ourselves, and that an attack of some description was inevitable unless they actually withdrew and ceased the activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree there were snipers in abundance on both sides?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Well, any soldier is a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Both sides carried out regular sniping activities aimed at the opposition, did they not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, sniping was a daily occurrence, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was indeed, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony regarding the military structure of the HVO armed forces and where the military police fit into that structure. I would like to ask you just a few questions in connection with that. I don't think there's any dispute about any of this, but tell me if there is. You found out, for example, that the Jokers sub-unit was actually an integral part of the military police, did you not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's what they told me themselves, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, based upon your conversation with the gentleman at the building, the Swiss-chalet-looking building that you mentioned, you travelled to Vitez and interviewed the civilian police there to find out who the commander was; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. That was during the early days. My assumption was to go to the only building I knew as the police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's exactly where they sent you, to the police headquarters; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Well, that was where I went because that was the only building I knew to have any involvement with the police at the time. I was then directed that the military police activity was coordinated at the Hotel Vitez, which is where I first met Mr. Santic, who was second in command to Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You say that you were sent over to the Hotel Vitez, and I believe one of the photographs that you were shown, Z2176, actually shows "Vojna Policija HVO" on the hotel. There was a big sign actually at the hotel announcing that that was the headquarters of the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not necessarily the headquarters, but that's where the military police -- some of the military police were situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's where you met the subordinate commander, the gentleman that you just identified?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: When I went to speak, they -- Mr. Santic introduced himself and was very reluctant to speak to me. I just introduced myself as the new liaison officer in the area, trying to got to know all the key figures to facilitate the U.N. mission, and he was indifferent. And we left it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's Mr. Vlado Santic as opposed to Mr. Ivica Santic, who was the mayor of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The gentlemen that you interviewed at the Swiss chalet were not actually wearing any insignia, patches, or badges, were they?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No. They were dressed in black combat gear, armed with various types of pistols, Uzis, Kalashnikovs, knives. One or two of them exhibited signs that they looked like they were involved -- they could have used at some point intravenous drugs. They had marks on their arms. They were all quite young, athletic, fit chaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to wind up this area of your testimony, it was clear to you that the gentleman that you've identified, Mr. Ljubicic, was the overall commander of the military police and all of their sub-units, including the Jokers; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that remained clear to you throughout your tour until November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was a fact that we confirmed at several points during the tour, that he was referred to as the head of the military police battalion, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You would agree that it is relatively common, in military units, for the military police headquarters to be located in the same place or building as the battalion headquarters, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: From a regular army point of view, military police are usually a high-level asset, and so it didn't surprise us at all that the military police battalion was co-located with 3rd Ops Zone command and Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there was no doubt in your mind that Colonel Blaskic, as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, had overall command of the assets in his theatre, including the military police?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As to his finite control over individual tasks, that was in question on one or two occasions because of the relationship with, for example, Mr. Cerkez. But we saw him as the overall strategic commander for HVO forces in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right, commanding all of the assets under his command, the brigades and the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You gave some testimony about a unit called the Vitezovi, commanded by Darko Kraljevic. Did you know that Darko Kraljevic was actually a colonel?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He referred to himself as Pukovnik Kraljevic. As to his official military rank, I don't know where you got the title "colonel" from, but, yes, that's how he liked to refer to himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just turn to the general command structure within the HVO armed forces as you perceived them, sir. You would agree that the principle of subordination is absolutely vital to the existence and functioning of any military chain of command, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Pretty much so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you did not encounter any problems passing checkpoints whenever you took Colonel Blaskic's liaison officer, Mr. Gelic, I believe you've identified him as, with you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Having Darko Gelic, Blaskic's LO, was a greater facilitator for moving around, but there were times when he himself, particularly when we were moving out of the area to the extremes of the Vitez area, I might run into problems. Either a local checkpoint commander would say, you know, "I'm not interested in what Blaskic or you have to say," you know, and the likes of the local battalion commander would be cited or the likes of Mr. Kordic or the brigade commander would be cited as the ultimate authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But generally speaking, when Mr. Gelic was present and gave an order, it was followed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, I would say 50/50, because I didn't actually use him on that many occasions. There was a few key issues when he proved to be useful, but there were also lot of occasions when he didn't seem to hold a lot of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In your view, the HVO had a very comprehensive command structure, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was a command structure that you would assume one would have in place, bearing in mind the number of troops, the circumstances they were in, and the fact that there were several professional ex-JNA soldiers occupying senior command appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic was an ex-JNA officer, was he not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he was, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so was General or Brigadier Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier Petkovic was the chief of the general staff of the HVO, with his headquarters in Mostar; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you, to be honest. But if that's the case, then it wouldn't surprise me. I was aware that he was a senior officer, superior to Colonel Blaskic, and was from out of the area, and I thought he was from Mostar. We referred to him as a general simply because it was the next rank up, but their rank structure terms are slightly different to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So from your perspective, as the Vitez liaison officer, Colonel Blaskic was the key military figure in the Lasva Valley area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All of the subordinate brigade commanders reported directly to him?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In theory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In general, did you not find that the HVO brigades were basically organised on the territorial principle, with members of the brigades coming from the local municipality?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And also men from a particular village would generally provide manpower for a company within the brigade, or a Sepnija [phoen] As it was called, I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't remember, to be honest, sir. But yes, that is how it works. There was basically the front line positions. Each brigade commander had his area for which he was responsible, and the local people formed the militia that maintained the defence of those lines. Any offensive military activity usually involved these groups they refer to as special forces, the likes of the Tvrtko, the Vitezovi or the Jokeri, and these were these mobile troops drafted from all over the place. They were well equipped and highly mobile and usually, it appeared to us, very well resourced and led by their own subordinate commanders, their own commanders, under the direction of various people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to use one example of the command relationship, you've identified Mr. Cerkez as the commander of the Viteska Brigade. One of his subordinate company commanders was Mr. Karlo Grabovac, I believe. Did you know the area for which Mr. Grabovac was responsible?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was [indiscernible] of the area around Rijeka up towards Kruscica area, so it was the southeastern portion in defence of the Vitez area, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one final question on this subject. Is it fair to say that at the end of the working day, the soldiers would go back to their own houses rather than the central barracks? At least you never saw a barracks while you were present; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were central training places, places like the wood yard, we used to house important resources at times. There were areas, blocks of flats, where large numbers of troops might be held, and I think those were the groups like the Jokeri or the Vitezovi that would take over and occupy certain areas. But the local militia obviously worked a duty system, duty rota, and returned to their own houses, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree that with respect to the men in the regular HVO brigades, they generally lived in their own houses and they did not live in a military barracks; isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And upon returning to their houses when they were off duty, they would take their weapons and uniforms with them, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It depended on the availability of weapons. Weapons could also be passed on to the chap taking over the duty. It would depend on the availability. People like the local militia didn't tend to have the pick and choice of weapons systems, whereas people like members of the Vitezovi, the specialist units, would have a couple of pistols and their own rifle and knives and all the rest of it, so they seemed to be well resourced as opposed to the local militia, who were just bearing a single firearm of some description.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You testified in the Blaskic case, at page 10.337 and 38, that generally the brigade members had their weapons and uniforms in their homes when they were not actively on duty, and you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. Like I said, there would be examples when depending on the availability of weapons, some would be handed over to the next guy on duty. But weapons were openly borne by everybody in the area if they had them available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony regarding Darko Kraljevic. I believe that you beat him in a pistol competition, and he awarded you a pistol as a result; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The first encounter with him, though, I imagine you remember particularly well because he held a gun up to your head, did he not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and also threatened to kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was on June the 11th or 12th, 1993, at around the time of the Convoy of Mercy or the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was around that time. It was the night when I had been asked by the colonel to go in and try and negotiate the release of the vehicles that had been captured. And at the time, I didn't know who it was at the time, but subsequently when I met him officially, his face was very familiar to me, and we laughed and joked about the incident retrospectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That incident involved ABiH mortaring, and everyone scattered after the mortar bombs began to fall; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that the Muslim forces in Stari Vitez had fired weapons into the Vitez area that night, on the night of the 10th of June, and actually killed eight little boys and girls?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of such. Had I received such information from the local Croats/HVO populous, that would have been included in the milinfosums that we published. There had been several instances where -- there was one particular one that I bore witness to because I was in the town at the time it was shelled, when the ABiH did actually shell at lunchtime period and several civilians, women, children and males, were injured during the shelling, and I was involved in moving them to the medical facility in the centre of Vitez. So it was a regular occurrence on both sides, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree that, as sad as it is, both sides had artillery assets and, unfortunately, used them regularly upon one another?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes, and we also had suspicions that when things were quiet from that point of view, that the Serbs would lob one in to kick them off firing at each other again. That was never proven, but it was a strong suspicion on our part, because it was to the Serbian advantage, obviously, that the conflict continued, as far as their intentions were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed that would be a significant tactical advantage to the Serbs, if you like, from doing that, since they were actually engaged in conflict with the ABiH and the HVO to the west and north of the town of Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Serbs suddenly had the artillery assets to be able to shell Vitez when and if they desired to do so; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We did employ forward air controllers who were specifically trained in the identification of that type of artillery fire, and it was never confirmed that that actually occurred, even though we specifically tasked troops with finding that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During the evening of June the 10th and the ensuing day, it's true that there were BBC film crews in the area actually filming events?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was press around us all the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few questions on Colonel Blaskic. His headquarters was in the Hotel Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And on the evening of June the 11th, the HVO headquarters was actually hit by artillery fire, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was in the building at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your view, the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was an active and well-informed commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, he appeared so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He appeared to have a comprehensive grasp of the military situation in his operative zone, at least in your view?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. He was mobile up and down the Lasva Valley. I came across him on a few occasions when he was in transitory headquarters, as it were, further up towards the Travnik area with specialist soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked this question by Judge Riad in the Blaskic case. You would certainly agree that he couldn't be reasonably viewed as a token or a puppet commander in any way, could he?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony regarding the military command structure in Vitez and Busovaca. I'm going to let Mr. Kovacic ask you about the structure in Vitez, but just a question or two regarding the Busovaca situation. It's true, is it not, that the commander of the HVO military forces in Busovaca was Commander Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed he's the gentleman that you identified as wearing the white T-shirt on Exhibit Z2546?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Correct, sir, Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't know if you can see it from here, but the gentleman sitting to his left is Darko Gelic, Colonel Blaskic's liaison officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Sir, that's wrong. It's the chap on the right in the T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recognise the fellow on the left here?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah. He was -- I can't remember his name. He was one of Grubesic's staff officers. On the two occasions I went to visit Grubesic, he was present with him, so I assumed he was a deputy commander of some description or a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for clearing that up. Mr. Grubesic was the commander of the brigade called the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade that was stationed in Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That sounds correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he reported to Colonel Blaskic as his commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In all likelihood, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You referred very briefly, in passing, to a gentleman with the nickname of Zuti. Do you remember him at all?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think I only met him once in passing, but he was quite well known in the Lasva Valley area by the locals and by -- I think Angus Hay met him on several occasions, as he was the liaison officer for that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to describe him as a fairly notorious mafioso who could generally be found involved in any of the mayhem that was going on in and around the Novi Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Like I say, I only had occasion to meet him. He seemed quite affable to me. We were sitting in a cafe at the time. So that would agree with the impressions that had been given by other people about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about the people shown in two photographs that were identified as Exhibits Z2510 and Z2509. I wonder if you could just get those in front of you, Mr. Whitworth. There were a lot of photographs there. All right. Just some questions in connection with the photograph that was marked as Z2509. Do you recognise the gentleman on the extreme right as Mr. Stipac, a politician from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Is this the chap in the white striped shirt?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't recognise him, no. The name sounds familiar, but it wasn't a character that I bumped into on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The gentleman that you identified as Mr. Kraljevic, who is next in from the left --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I didn't actually identify him as -- I said the quality of the photograph wasn't distinct but that could have been him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The photograph is pretty indistinct, sir, but let me just ask you to take a close look at it and suggest to you that that's actually Zoran Kapetanovic who was Colonel Blaskic's personal bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It could have been. I could have been mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In the front row, the next person over in the striped shirt, do you recognise that gentleman as Mr. Spajic, a politician from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, it was out of my area of responsibility, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And the gentleman on the left-hand side in the purple shirt, carrying a briefcase, do you recognise that as Mr. Niko Grubesic, a politician from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Which photograph are we looking at now?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I see a purple shirt. I'm slightly colour-blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Is it this gentleman here you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Looking at Exhibit Z2510, immediately to the left of Mr. Santic, who you have identified as the mayor of Vitez, do you recognise that gentleman as Mr. Zoran Maric, the president of the HVO government in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Which gentleman are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The gentleman in the dark suit carrying a briefcase.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise the gentleman. I didn't come across him at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever meet any of the local politicians in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I didn't, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I spent a very brief period of time there just arranging meetings between Colonel Alastair and Mr. Kordic on one or two occasions, and I stood in there a week while Boris was away on R & R. But other than that, let's say, it was out of my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to Mr. Anto Valenta, you have given some testimony about this gentleman. Do you know what his political position was throughout the time that you were present in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Other than knowing he was a key political figure, when I first met him, I wasn't aware of who he was. I was just introduced to him, or he, rather, on being aware of my presence in the building, introduced himself to me and we sat down and had a conversation, and he ran through his ideas of how things were going to take place in the Lasva Valley pocket. But I wasn't aware of who he was until I'd reported back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was his political position?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he was a senior member of the Croatian government of some description. I can't quite remember which political affiliation he was part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You saw him in the same building as Colonel Blaskic, in the Hotel Vitez, on occasion, I believe?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your view was that Mr. Valenta was superior to Mr. Kordic; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was the impression that we had, yes, over a period of time, was that Mr. Kordic was, shall we say, an understudy to Mr. Valenta; i.e., on Mr. Valenta's departure, Mr. Kordic was the key political figure in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, you've said that, but where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Just -- it was based on the fact that people commented on Mr. Kordic's authority and influence in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Valenta say that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall doing so, having only met him twice and at the beginning of the tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Mr. Kordic say that he was the understudy or subordinate to Mr. Valenta politically?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Colonel Blaskic ever describe the relationship between Mr. Valenta and Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't say I did, no. I think one of the -- I think Colonel Alastair, as he was then, is probably better qualified to make comment on that, as he had more personal conversations with Mr. Kordic and might have better recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, though, that your information was that Mr. Valenta was the most senior political Croatian figure in the Lasva Valley; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you say that he left Vitez at some point; did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When did he leave?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: During the U.N.-arranged meeting in Kiseljak when we provided all the armoured vehicles, escorts, Mr. Valenta didn't come back. He left then, along with Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic and the people that you saw there on the list. There were, if my memory serves me correctly, I did a head count; there were eight people who didn't come back. From the approximately 25 people that we took, there was two or three Warriors with nobody left in at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have talked about that meeting; do you recall when that meeting actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it was quite early on in the tour. I think it was around the beginning of June time, maybe. I was still feeling my way, getting to know the key personalities. Hence, as far as I was concerned, I was familiar with Mr. Skopljak, Mr. Santic, as the key civilian authorities in the area, and wasn't aware of the military people as such. We were trying to deal at that level to start off with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that prominent Croat politicians from the Lasva Valley area had been helicoptered by UNPROFOR from Kiseljak to the town of Medjugorje at the end of August of 1993 for the inauguration of an entity known as the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that -- well, I don't recall it. It was probably given to us at a briefing at the end of the day, but no, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The pictures that you spoke about or that you identified showing Mr. Kordic specifically, do you know when they were taken?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Again, it's at the same time that we arranged the meeting in Kiseljak, and I'm surprised that there is not a date in the milinfosums detailing that particular meeting. But I would have thought it was around June time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it possible, sir, that it would have been at the end of August?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Sir, my recollection, chronologically, of events is not perfect, bearing in mind the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to one other subject now, the defence of Stari Vitez about which you testified. There's no question that the Muslim commander in Stari Vitez, Sefkija Dzidic, was in communication with the 325th Mountain Brigade headquarters in Kruscica, is there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, he was in direct communication with them, and as a consequence, probably to 3 Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Dzidic was able to call down mortar and artillery support from ABiH positions above Vitez whenever there was an attack on Stari Vitez, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wouldn't have said that was the case, no. There were occasions when mortars and artillery fell on Vitez, and I would doubt very much whether the plight of the people in Stari Vitez would have held that much sway on the decision to use resources as important and scarce as artillery and mortars by 325 Brigade, but there were instances when activity in Stari Vitez corresponded to when shells and mortars, which is what they usually were, were falling in Vitez centre itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You and your colleagues concluded that military and other supplies must have been getting through to Stari Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We suspected that there must have been, but that was not based on any observation. There were actually -- they did have a stockpile of munitions in Stari Vitez, because during the initial conflict, when the Croats and Muslims were resisting the Serb push down the valley initially, they were actually fighting on the same side, and Stari Vitez is an old part, big cellars, et cetera, and so there'd been weapons stockpiled in there. There must have -- we strongly suspect there must have been a trickle of some description getting in somehow; hence it was finding the 7,62 millimetre round cartons in the -- wrapped up in the bandages that got in on that particular occasion. But it must have only been a trickle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It is true that the Croats made several offers to the citizens of Stari Vitez to permit civilians to be evacuated, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was an offer made that civilians could leave, but as the situation in Stari Vitez was the same as in Vitez itself, is that the local -- the militia were local people that would be giving up their homes and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt you, but it was a pretty simple question. The Croats did make several offers to citizens of Stari Vitez to permit civilians to be evacuated. That is true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can recall one such instance when an offer was made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked on page 10.375 of the Blaskic transcript: "During your tour of duty, did you become familiar with the offers made by the Croat community in Vitez to the citizens of Stari Vitez to temporarily evacuate Stari Vitez and get out of the war zone?" And your answer was: "Yes, I was aware of those offers."

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And those offers were actually rejected, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: For the reason I was trying to elaborate to earlier, that the people defending Stari Vitez were actually the occupants of Stari Vitez. They were the militia on the same base that the people in Vitez were militia; i.e., they lived there and didn't see why they had to give up their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You never, yourself, saw any "bebes," I think they were called, b-e-b-e-s, fall on Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Mirad showed me the one that I took the photograph of. I came across the ironmonger that was welding the base plates in Vitez where they were making the launch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, simple question: You didn't actually see any fall in Stari Vitez, did you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No. Heard a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You, yourself, were permitted by the HVO to evacuate a number of old and injured people from Stari Vitez, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can you -- I can't recall -- I can recall doing so, but are you referring to a particular example?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you testified in the Blaskic case, on page 10.443: "We were eventually allowed to remove maybe a dozen or so people who were old or injured or required regular medical attention that they couldn't get within the limited confines of Stari Vitez."

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You -- sorry, Mr. Whitworth, the translator says the response was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Would you like to repeat the question? I'll repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've had enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, have you got much more, Mr. Sayers, for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would think, Your Honour, I have about another 40 minutes, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, because we must try and finish him today. He's been brought here from his duties in England, and it's not right that he should be kept here longer than today, so could you speed up, please.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the smuggling incident that you have previously testified about involving commander Dzidic in Stari Vitez, you actually confronted him personally about being tricked and deceived into being used as a conduit for ammunition into Stari Vitez; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He basically shrugged his shoulders and said, "What do you expect"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, he told you that these things were necessary; right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, he could well have done. I remember him saying that -- you know, in his position, you couldn't expect him to do anything else, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few questions in connection with the Convoy of Mercy or the Convoy of Joy incident. It's true -- and I don't think there is any dispute about this -- that there was a major Muslim offensive underway on the town of Travnik in the period June the 8th through June the 12th of 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The dates escape me, but there was a major ABiH offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say that the HVO was defeated in Travnik and that the town was captured by ABiH forces; right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The HVO -- yeah, withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that there were many thousands of refugees that came out of the town as a result?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I didn't bear witness to that many, but I'm sure there were quite a few, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Convoy of Joy was actually a purely private convoy; it was not a UNHCR- or U.N.-sponsored convoy at all, was it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah. It was done on the initiative of -- the name of the town up north escapes me, but it was done on the initiative of the local people, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, it was Tuzla. That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the mandate of the BritBat forces in Nova Bila and in the Lasva Valley area was to facilitate the passage of humanitarian aid through U.N.-sponsored agencies, was it not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe that's part of the mandate, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And are you aware of several Croats having been shot to death during the Convoy of Joy incident by UNPROFOR forces?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was a conflict that arose, I think, at the time the decision was taken by Colonel Alastair that minimum force was needed to try and prevent further deterioration of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that involved the death of several Croats, did it not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't tell you as to how many, but there was one or two -- there was a few people killed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the Convoy of Joy incident, you would agree that there is no mention of Mr. Kordic's name in connection with that episode as related by you in your statement of August the 14th, 1996, is there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Without referring to the statement, probably not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We can put the pertinent page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to do that; I'm sure the witness will accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is no doubt about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The reference, as I recollect, to him, came, did it not, in a milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You did not give any testimony in connection with Mr. Kordic, insofar as the Convoy of Joy incident is related, in the Blaskic case, did you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think I was concentrating on Colonel Blaskic's part in the thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the same is true in the Kupreskic case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He probably wasn't asked about this.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wasn't, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, this isn't being very helpful at the moment. The reference is in the milinfosum. If you've got a question about that, ask it, Mr. Sayers; otherwise, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the apprehension of the convoy, it was actually stopped by a large crowd of Croat civilian women and children, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes, it was. I didn't bear witness to it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the presence of Ambassador Thebault, in your view, caused immediate action on the part of Colonel Blaskic to order the release of the convoy, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Ambassador Thebault had been brought into the area on short notice to try and assist in resolving the situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On page 3 of your 1996 statement, you say: "I also clearly recall that the presence of Thebault caused immediate action on the part of Blaskic to order the release of the convoy."

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's accurate, is it not? All right. I think that you testified in the Blaskic case that based upon orders issued by Colonel Blaskic, Mr. Gelic, his liaison officer, and you were successful in getting a large number of vehicles released so that the convoy could actually continue on to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Eventually, yes, we went and trolled around the area, collecting vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All of the local HVO commanders obeyed Colonel Blaskic's orders as relayed to them by Mr. Gelic, did they not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This is after the incident at the Dubravica checkpoint with Commander Cerkez and when Karlo Grabovac was present. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you testified in the Blaskic case that because of the problems, you decided to go straight to the top and deal with the head man; right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the head man was Colonel Blaskic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As the overall military commander on the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, were you actually present when either General Petkovic or Mr. Kordic or any other military or political figure was involved in the negotiations relating to this incident?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was present -- General Petkovic wasn't there. I was present when Mr. Kordic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the civilian crowd that apprehended the convoy and stopped it and looted it was highly agitated, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, shells were falling in the centre of Vitez as this convoy was being apprehended; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no. You're talking about a different instance. The Convoy of Joy, to the best of my recollection, was unimpeded by artillery or mortar fire, whereas that did occur when the U.N. vehicles were held in the centre of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the milinfosum that you authored, Z1044, number 43, did you actually author the comment that is contained on page 1 of the document?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Which one are we referring to again? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's 1PWA milinfosum number 43, looking particularly at the comment that appears in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, the comment comes from the intelligence officer who's drawn in all the experiences and the witness accounts from the liaison officers throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who the intelligence officer was?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Captain Simon Harrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Simon Harrison, and that's his conclusion, I take it.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. It would have been based on information that we'd have fed in to him and our opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anybody tell you that Mr. Kordic had taken any part in the planning of that convoy apprehension?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't have any recollection of such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Certainly Colonel Blaskic never said any such thing, did he?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't have any recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kordic didn't while you were present at the negotiation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think I've stated on several occasions I don't have any specific recollection about the conversations at the time. I was more interested in physically getting the convoy back together and facilitating its safe passage on. And it was Colonel Alistair who was chairing the meetings and discussions with Blaskic and Mr. Kordic at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would that be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, if you and Mr. Kovacic could so organise the time between you that the witness finishes this afternoon, that would be useful and also necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I fully understand, Mr. President, and I will do my level best to ensure that that occurs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Whitworth, we're going to adjourn now until half past 2.00. Please don't speak to anybody about your evidence during the adjournment and any others there may be. Don't let anybody else speak to you about it, and that includes the members of the Prosecution. Half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Whitworth.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In keeping with the Presiding Judge's instructions, I'm going to try to be through with you in about 20 minutes, if I can, so let me just cover a few topics that you raised during your direct examination with some degree of alacrity. The incident in which Ms. Kolaba was shot on July the 5th, 1993, she was actually shot as she was inside the house in which you were, I believe, as a --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A round actually went through a wall and hit her in the head and killed her; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's not correct, sir, no. She stood in a doorway to the house when a round went through her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you did a three- to four-day investigation yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: With the assistance of HVO representatives provided by -- I think they were from the Vitez Brigade, at Colonel Blaskic's initiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the Blaskic case, you described this incident by saying that several rounds hit the side of the buildings, and one of the rounds was the one that went through Ms. Kolaba's head and killed her. Were you actually upstairs or downstairs at the time the incident occurred, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I stood on the balcony above her when the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you actually see the incident?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wasn't actually looking at the firing point, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe that your commanding officer, Colonel Duncan, actually tasked you to head up an investigative team to find out what had happened, and you conducted a three-day investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And reached no definitive conclusions, I take it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The conclusion that I reached, along with members of our own military police who assisted, was that the firing point was from one of the Croat houses on the opposite side of the road to where we were actually located.
