utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During the course of your investigation, you tried to enlist the assistance of the 325th Mountain Brigade personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you found them to be not particularly cooperative; isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You're not saying that Ms. Kolaba was deliberately targeted; she was just an unfortunate victim in the middle of a firefight. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think as I described in the Colonel Blaskic case, there was a small-arms exchange taking place at the time, and Colonel Alastair's intent was that somebody would be brought to justice for it, because it had been deliberately -- the small-arms exchange had taken place in an area that was known to occupy [sic] U.N. troops, and she was effectively a U.N. employee at the time. We had made several attempts to broker local ceasefire agreements to protect -- for the safety of our own people, and that obviously wasn't the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever share the results of your investigation with the HVO, or the ABiH, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did indeed, sir, yes. I didn't share them with the ABiH, because of their indifference at the time, but I shared them with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With whom did you do that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was with Darko Gelic, because the report went back to Colonel Blaskic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to the second incident that you described, the shooting of the UNHCR driver, isn't it true that you attempted to gain admission to Stari Vitez to investigate the actual point of impact but that commander Dzidic prohibited anyone from entering Stari Vitez to investigate the impact point?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I actually stood at the impact point. The impact point was a road junction on the way to commander Sefkija's house. So that's not correct, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On page 10.264 of the Blaskic case, you said that the investigation quickly ground to a halt because commander Sefkija, the BiH commander in Stari Vitez, would not let any member of the HVO enter the area to investigate the impact point.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes. You asked me about my access to the impact area, and that wasn't denied at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. With respect to helicopters, did you ever see the markings on any helicopter?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The ones that landed at Kiseljak were not -- didn't have any military insignia on them. They were simply plain, with a blue stripe down. They were similar markings to the ones we'd seen in Split, and also were similar in markings to the ones, as best we could identify, as they came into motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The testimony that you gave about assumptions that these helicopters were used to carry people of importance are just that, assumptions, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It's an assumption, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In all of your six months in the theatre, you never saw any evidence of civilians being used to dig trenches, did you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not -- no, sir, not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have referred to Mr. Kordic's offices as located in a building called the Eagle's Nest. Who called it that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was just a nickname passed on to me by the Busovaca LO. I'm not quite sure where he picked up the title from. I think it was -- I got the impression, when I visited it on the one occasion that I did, that it was because of its situation. It was down the end of a very quiet, isolated valley as you went in towards the mountains out of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any other Eagle's Nests?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a building in Vares referred to by the NordBat commander as Eagle's Nest?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the building referred to as the Wolf's Lair, as opposed to the Eagle's Nest?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a couple of concluding questions regarding Mr. Kordic. Do you know what his position within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't. I don't know what his particular political affiliation was or of which party, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether he ever had a position within the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not officially, sir, no, I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall that Croat politicians and military leaders held regular press conferences in the summer of 1993, sir? Weekly, in fact?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In all likelihood they did, but I can't recall any of such that spring to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall ever attending any of them?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That concludes the questions I had, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sayers. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Whitworth, my name is Bozidar Kovacic. I'm a lawyer from Rijeka, and Mr. Mikulicic and I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez. The problem of interpretation or, rather, the language, continues to be topical, even though we speak different languages, and we have to be slow enough so that the interpreters can follow us. Of course, if you fail to understand any one of the questions, please tell me so, and I shall repeat it. You are a captain, aren't you, by rank?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was indeed, sir, at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, because of the linguistic problems, is it true that in your daily communication with the HVO, and I suppose the BH army as well, that you used a nickname, "Perry"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So can I then assume that the local HVO commanders, and that is what I should like to know, who communicated with you that knew you by that nickname?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was my first name, and it was used. I was referred to as "Captain Perry" by all the people I knew in Bosnia, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, a few questions about the convoy that you dwelt in considerable detail on, because I'm not quite sure that everything is quite clear and to avoid any misunderstanding. Reports mention three names given that convoy. In some places, it is called the Convoy of Joy, then a Convoy of Mercy, and the third term applied to the convoy is the Tuzla Convoy. But do all these names refer to one and the same convoy?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, sir, yes, that's the case. The Convoy of Joy was the name that we in BritBat referred to the convoy by. I think the Convoy of Mercy was one used frequently by the press. And the Tuzla reference, of course, was the one used by members of the convoy themselves because that was their origin, although I think there was more than one convoy that originated from Tuzla and so it's quite possible that different names were used. But this particular reference is about the major, long, 80-vehicle convoy that was transiting from Split up to Tuzla. We referred to it as the Convoy of Joy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there is no doubt that it happened on the 10th/11th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My specific recollections of dates are very hazy as a consequence of the time that's passed since. The best reference from which to draw those conclusions are the milinfosums, as they were completed on a daily basis, and so they are probably, in some cases, a better recollection of what actually happened than I might give when referring to specific dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Of course, quite reasonable. Milinfosums do mention the 10th and 11th of June, saying that a convoy had reached Central Bosnia on those two dates. The convoy itself, according to the information available, first General Petkovic that you mentioned, as it was being prepared, had personally promised -- had personally given his word that that convoy would be allowed to pass through. Did you have that information at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I might have done so, but I don't recall at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That convoy was first blocked in the Novi Travnik area; is that correct? That is when the difficulties began?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think that's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so when the difficulties began, do you know that at some point in time, General Petkovic was in Vitez and that negotiations were conducted then and contacts were established with the highest-ranking UNPROFOR officers or, rather, ECMM representatives so as to resolve the situation after the convoy was intercepted in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't have any specific recollection about that. My recollections cover only those that involved with BritBat, where Colonel Alastair was involved and Ambassador Thebault at the time. I was unaware if General Petkovic was involved or, rather, I can't remember him being involved at any stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm looking at an ECMM report of the 13th of July, 1993 -- 13th of June, and it has "4040" on page 5. The author of that part of the report says that he will go to Vitez and try to talk to General Petkovic, who spent the night there. That note refers to the 10th of June, and the subtitle is "HVO Attack on the Tuzla Convoy," although you do not remember whether Mr. Petkovic was there or not. But those negotiations were conducted at a very high level, one might say. Don't you think so?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would say so, yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it a military standard that the highest-ranking officer on the ground at the time takes over the principal role or has the main say in whatever negotiations?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. There's no reason why -- if he's the executive officer present, then obviously his subordinates would fall in line with his wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In relation to those negotiations, the solution that was arrived at was that the convoy should be put together again so as to proceed on its way in the area near the Impregnacija factory, that is, on the outskirts, on the edge of the town of Vitez, the Impregnacija where they treated timber for the use by railways or whatever, and that is where the convoy was put together, where everybody gathered? But will you please not just nod your head but tell us "Yes" or "No" for the record?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was where a major obstacle prevented the convoy moving on, in terms of there was a large collection of the civilian population, and it was at the Dubravica checkpoint adjacent to that wood yard that you're referring that the confrontation took place between Commander Cerkez, with Ambassador Thebault present, and Colonel Blaskic. As far as the vehicles being present at that point, they weren't -- they had been distributed, disseminated, through the Vitez town itself and were at various points along the road, and on the agreement that the civilian population should break up and move away sometime later, it was at that point that we started moving vehicles back together and forming packets of vehicles to form the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So we agree that that was where an attempt was made to form the convoy again so that it could proceed on its way?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was where the final obstacle occurred. Once that had been removed, then it allowed, as I said, the packets of vehicles to be formed and to move up on the road towards the Zenica area and out of the Lasva Valley area. But the convoy wasn't actually formed up at that point. That was just the last major barrier to the convoy's reformation and subsequent movement out of the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So the chief obstacle -- the chief difficulty originated with civilians, you said. Did they put forward some reasons, I mean those civilians who were protesting for some reason or another, did they explain, give you some reasons why they were opposed to the reformation of the convoy and its further movement?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The comment that was repeated was that the contents of the convoy should be targeted equally to the Lasva-Vitez area as well as to the Tuzla area. There were no militia or soldiers present in these groups of people blocking. They were ostensibly just women and children; i.e., people whom we, as soldiers, have great difficulty in moving or getting to break up to allow a convoy to move on. There was a notable absence of any militia in the area where all this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But, at that time, in Vitez and around it, in the Lasva Valley, all the difficulties notwithstanding, there was some civilian police, wasn't there, and you had the opportunity to see them?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was two members of the civilian police, that's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you mention that site, because that school in Dubravica is only a little bit further away, it was where the Vitezovi unit, Darko Kraljevic's unit, had its headquarters. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that particular location, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You did not know it, identify it, as one of the places where they met?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you repeat the question, please? I didn't understand whether I did or I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No. I was only asking if you were aware that that was one of their meeting places, not the principal meeting place, but one of their meeting places.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure which particular building and area you're referring to. There was an area on towards Nova Bila that's like a short block of flats that I know had been used for meetings between Colonel Blaskic and various other military commanders, but the only confirmed location I'm aware of that the Vitezovi had was towards the end of the tour when they used the place in Gornji Vecerska. They obviously had their headquarters somewhere else prior to that, but I was unaware of any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned the presence of Cerkez among those civilians. Are you saying that he was issuing orders, that he was commanding those civilians in any way, that they were, to all intents and purposes, under his control, subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I'm just saying that there was a notable absence of any military or civil presence who could have taken -- made efforts to take the situation in hand there to support Colonel Blaskic, and I think that was the basis of Colonel Blaskic's reprimand, or what appeared to me a reprimand as far as I was concerned, when he espied Commander Cerkez doing nothing to facilitate the carrying out of Blaskic's orders in the removal of the blockade, the blockade to the convoy, and the reformation of the convoy. There was little or -- there was no involvement of the civilian police. There was no involvement of the militia. As I said earlier, there was a notable absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When Blaskic spoke to Cerkez, did you surmise -- did you assume that you knew the contents of their conversation on the basis of their gestures and their faces or did somebody tell you about what they had talked about?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To me, it was surmised by myself at the time that the body language, the terms with which Colonel Blaskic spoke to Commander Cerkez, Commander Cerkez's reaction, was that Blaskic was reprimanding him or verbally cajoling him into supporting Colonel Blaskic's orders in terms of having the human blockade removed to allow the convoy to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does that mean that you think that a Domobran, a home guard unit, an HVO unit, was responsible for the control of order and civilian conduct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can you repeat which unit, please, you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Any HVO unit. Or this brigade, do you think that it is responsible for controlling and establishing order among civilians?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would have expected that the military hold considerable power and influence over the local population, bearing in mind the circumstances in the Lasva Valley. Commander Cerkez was highly respected by the Croat population in Vitez. There were civilian police present who were recognised as a suitable authority at the Dubravica checkpoint. As most of the male population of a serving age were members of the local militia and therefore under the command of Commander Cerkez, it seemed that he would be an influential figure able to support Colonel Blaskic's aims of allowing the convoy to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You said that there was an insignificant number of HVO soldiers, so even if this was Cerkez's duty, how could he do anything about those civilians, that is, make them disperse, and take over or something?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: For the reasons that I stated earlier. Firstly, he was a well respected and well known local figure in Vitez whom people referred to, and, secondly, it wouldn't have been unreasonable, if he was supporting Colonel Blaskic's aims, to have local militia there that would lend support to what should have happened in terms of the blockade being removed. Likewise, the civilian police were there as well, who should have been -- I have no doubt were informed of the situation and should also have been supporting the control of the human blockade, and that would have helped greatly in facilitating the removal of the blockade and the movement of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe we've rounded off this part. Now, if I may draw your attention to another subject about which I should like to ask you several questions, something that has to do with the chain of command. In some place, you say that Cerkez looked like the commander of all HVO units in Vitez, but let us try to establish certain facts. HVO brigades were formed on the territorial principle and they were associated with the municipalities in which they were formed; is that true?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that for instance in Busovaca -- no, sorry -- well, in Busovaca and in Vitez, in both those places, in the same, therefore, Operative Zone, and they had one and the same commander, not to mention other adjacent municipalities. I'm trying to simplify matters. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: From a simplistic point of view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Specifically in Busovaca, Mr. Grubesic is the commander of the local brigade there, and you spoke about him, and in Vitez, it is Mario Cerkez. We've also talked about them, and both of them are subordinated to Blaskic as the commander of the Operative Zone; there are no doubts about that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Are you asking -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it appeared to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your testimony, you also said that the Jokers unit which was in Busovaca was not under Grubesic's command, who was the brigade commander in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct. I think the commander of the military police, Pasko Ljubicic, had overall command of the Jokeri.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Jokers were a special-purpose unit of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Of the military police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But Vitezovi were another special unit within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think they were members of the military police as such; they were a specialist unit of the HVO. "Special forces," they liked to refer to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it logical then, that Blaskic should apply the same model of organisation or the chain of command to Busovaca, Vitez, and probably other locales under his command?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Which particular bit are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm specifically referring to the fact that if, in Busovaca, the brigade commander is not in command of a special unit, then obviously that cannot be the case in Vitez either, or vice versa. If he is in command of a special unit, then he must be in other places too, because they all belong to the same zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's not true, sir, no. Basically a military unit is made up of regular militia units, and within a large corps or divisional structure, based on formal army structure, there will be specialist units within that. The responsibilities and command for those units can be delegated by the high commander, i.e., Colonel Blaskic, to his subordinate commanders in order to effect particular military operations. I speak -- based on my own experiences, for example, we have specialist engineers, we have our own special forces, and they will be attached -- detached from one commander and attached to another in order to effect a successful military operation in particular areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, have you ever seen an order from which it is possible to infer that the Vitezovi was subordinate to the brigade, that they were a special unit within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The command would not be delegated as a subordinate. The expertise and knowledge of one commander would be used alongside with the local commander's knowledge to achieve an aim, and so a -- for example, a specialist engineer commander, who might only be a captain, would be the chief advisor to a colonel undertaking a particular task involving engineering. So we envisaged similar relationships occur within the specialist units of the HVO structure, where commanders such as Kraljevic would be used, and his specialism and expertise and familiarity of his men and soldiers would be used alongside with the local knowledge of a commander. I'm confident, Kraljevic, his ego wouldn't allow him to be subordinate to the likes of commander Cerkez anyway, and as it's not a formal army structure, it's more a collegiate affair in such operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Document Z1087, milinfosum number 52, dated the 20th of June: Do you have it in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In Z1087, I should like to draw your attention to paragraph number 10, section B. You use here, obviously, an example of the existence of special units, or independent units, as they are called here, under the command of Blaskic. Among others that are mentioned here, the Vitezovi are specified. According to a normal military structure and the theory of chain of command, the higher commander with his written orders is addressing lower-level units under his direct command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: You could say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If the Vitezovi are subordinated on a permanent basis to the brigade, would Blaskic then be addressing the Vitezovi with his written orders?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Specialist units like that would never be permanently detached. They were what we refer to as mobile surgical forces, who were very mobile and used for particular jobs, and so would remain under the constant command of Colonel Blaskic, but whom, for periods of time, would be delegated for the use of brigade commanders. The likes of the Vitez Brigade, which was under a lot of pressure at the time, which is a key geographical area in the 3rd Op Zone, bearing in mind the proximity of headquarters, that would be what we classify as a main effort, and therefore resources such as specialist units would be farmed out to the local commanders on the ground to help them substantiate and maintain their current position if under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us mention in passing, in June or July, during your tour of duty as a liaison officer in that area, did you have occasion to see that all units operating in Vitez had a certain area of responsibility regarding holding the front lines against the adversary, each had a specific area of responsibility, each individual unit? Did you have occasion to see that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was aware that there were essentially brigade areas, and there were at times points that were very volatile because of the level of confrontation between the BiH where the front line positions were substantiated, the local militia positions were substantiated with such troops as the Vitezovi, in order to repel any further military action in that particular area. As for the existence of regular defensive lines occupied by the likes of the Vitezovi and the 4th Military Police Battalion, I'm not aware of any such existence. To the best of my knowledge, we were always of the opinion that, as I said earlier, they were mobile forces committed in response to offensive military plans or to substantiate defence during times of particularly aggressive action by the ABiH in certain areas of the valley, as any commander would do to maintain a flexible response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague, defence counsel for Mr. Kordic, mentioned something, and I would like to follow on to that. During your stay in Central Bosnia, did you notice that the Vitez Brigade had any kind of training grounds or compound where the troops were housed, except for the cinema building where the headquarters was?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I have a photograph here somewhere showing a group of 30 troops amassed and marching along the main street by Nova Bila. There was a young training -- a group of young soldiers, and they were brought together for training. I don't know whether they actually resided in a building that formed a training establishment or whether they were just part of the young militia being trained upon a daily basis, which would be perfectly understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sir, my question had to do with Vitez municipality. Nova Bila is another municipality; that is Novi Travnik. I'm talking about Vitez municipality and the Vitez Brigade. Did you ever see any kind of base or compound where troops of the Vitez Brigade were using -- which they were using as a barracks or a training centre, some kind of buildings or facilities where they were based? I'm talking about the Vitez Brigade exclusively.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir. As we talked earlier, they were all local militia as such, and under the circumstances, it would have been quite foolhardy to house them all in one building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Earlier, using the term "local militia," you said that when they were not on the front, they were allowed to go home. You did have occasion to see that and to realise that for yourself?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, there were occasions when I met troops, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your testimony, you mentioned that Darko Kraljevic used the term "colonel" to describe himself, and that is how others addressed him, I think. Tell us, please, did you ever hear Cerkez having a rank, or anyone addressing him by rank?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, other than "commander," which is a generic term.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So they addressed him using the generic term, but you never heard his rank being used?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was, as far as we were concerned, commonly known as the brigade commander for Vitez Brigade, and we just referred to him as "commander Cerkez."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The rank of colonel in any army is a very senior rank, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Subordinate to brigade commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Following on that logic, the brigade commander would have to have a rank above colonel?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A brigade commander is a brigadier. But the rank structure we became aware of in the HVO paralleled our own experiences in some cases and not in others. In terms of -- we tended to name people in terms of their -- the command of their geographical area and the number of troops under command, and hence, why it was called the Vitez Brigade. It was approximately a brigade area, and the term "brigada" was used by the HVO themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Since you mentioned this, you're aware that the surrounding brigades in places around Vitez had a name usually taken from history, of a historical figure, and it was only the Viteska Brigade, as you called it, was officially called the Viteska Brigade, the brigade belonging to town of Vitez. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's very interesting. I wasn't aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you had to use the services of an interpreter, did you ever have the problem of the two terms being confused, the Vitezovi and the Viteska Brigade, as the root word is the same?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, the interpreters we employed were both Croat Muslim, and in Dobrila's case, Serbian, and the Vitezovi was a significant name which everybody was familiar with, and so there was no danger of confusion on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have several questions regarding the patients who were transferred from Stari Vitez that you referred to. Towards the end of the cross, you said that they had been held in the basement of a building. Do you know where the reserve position was of the medical centre, in a basement of a building in the very centre of town? Did you ever have occasion to visit it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I took several casualties there during a mortar attack on one particular occasion. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is this the place you're referring to when you say that those two people were detained there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My recollection is not as such, no, but it's -- my recollection is not particularly good about that particular issue. It could have been, but I do have distinct memory that one of them was being held in a cellar area of some description.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the other one was at home?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall where the second one was. They were held separately. One of them might have actually been held in the hospital, but one was definitely held in a cellar. I can picture it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Apart from this medical centre that you said you visited, were there any other medical facilities in Vitez that were operational at the time in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was the hospital church at Nova Bila, but that's not part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's Nova Bila, but not in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The one I'm familiar with is the one that was underneath the -- I think it's like a shopping arcade, underneath, down in what looked like some cleared-out cellars. It was an improvised medical centre for treating people in Vitez, and a lot of medical treatment was given there to the local people which ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So in fact that was a cellar, a basement?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not the likes of which I'm thinking about. It was very large, open, white painted, with pillars inside it. I have quite a distinct recollection about that particular type of building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With windows at the top, level with the ground, if you can recollect that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. I do also recall that initially, when the two Muslims were taken from the ICRC, I visited them in the Nova Bila hospital initially, if my memory serves me correctly, where they were initially checked by the medical and surgical staff at Nova Bila hospital and it was 28 -- 48 hours later that I revisited one of them, one of -- the other one could have been kept in the medical facility we were referring to in Vitez but my recollection is vague, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, since you mentioned the Nova Bila hospital, can it be said to have been in good shape?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it was an outstanding achievement by the local medical staff who'd erected a hospital there. It was far from ideal. They were working under very difficult circumstances, and treated a lot of casualties and did a lot of good work there. Hence our -- my involvement in trying to secure regular evacuation from the area. They were working under very difficult circumstances there and were poorly equipped, despite help from us in the ICRC, to deal with the number and the nature of some of the casualties that they received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let us go back to the exchange. Actually, the agreement on one exchange between the two parties had already been underway when this request of the Red Cross appeared for these two patients, and through your mediation, you heard and understood that an exchange had already been negotiated, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's not -- not as far as I remember. My recollection is that I'd been taken to see a family whose three sons, age range from 10 to 14 years, had been captured by the BiH whilst involved in some farming or collection activity. Commander Cerkez appealed to me to try and identify the whereabouts of these three children. I went to -- I was allowed passage to Kruscica to do so. I visited the three boys. I think the ICRC had also visited them, and then at some point during the proceedings before we'd managed to secure an exchange, these two people were -- two Muslims were removed from the ICRC one particular evening as they were departing Stari Vitez and subsequently when I talked with commander Cerkez and the local authorities with reference to them releasing these two people who were chronically ill in one case back into the hands of the ICRC stating quite clearly that what they had done was unacceptable. What was offered to me was to secure the exchange and release of these three young boys and then the two members taken from the ICRC would be released. That's my recollection. That's not quite what transpired or nearly didn't transpire towards the end when on the day that I actually had arranged the exchange. Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher for his assistance for us to distribute a document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D41/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The English translation is on the second page. When you look at the date, which you couldn't see before, does it correspond, does this jog your memory? I should like to draw your attention to the persons mentioned under 6, 7, and 8, with the date of birth indicated. Could they be the boys you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They could indeed, sir, yes. I would think that they are, bearing in mind the ages. That corresponds with my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is a document that you did not have occasion to see during those contacts and negotiations when you were trying to agree on the exchange?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I haven't seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your testimony, you mentioned Mr. Borislav Jozic, who was killed and whom you described as an honourable person who was held in high esteem. Did you have occasion to meet or hear about Stipo Krizanac?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In all likelihood, I did meet him, but I don't have any recollection. I met an awful lot of people whilst I was out there, and it being so long ago, my recollection of names is just the key figures, limited to the key personnel whom I saw on a very regular basis or who were obviously key to the functioning of the BritBat unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, understandably so. I was just checking to see whether perhaps you still remembered the name. I should now like to go on to the issue of Grbavica, even though it has been discussed at length, but I have only a few brief questions for the sake of clarification. Can we agree that the described position of the ABiH army at Grbavica, in military terms, was of strategic importance for the very forces that wanted to have control of the road running through the valley between the town and Bila?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. It is of strategic importance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were aware that until Grbavica fell, that is, until the HVO captured Grbavica, the only route going from the town towards the hospital at Nova Bila, for instance, was a roundabout dirt road rather than the main road?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been the road round back of Mose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was a dirt road, wasn't it? Most of it did not have an asphalt cover?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No. It was regularly transited by the likes of myself in a Land Rover. It was easily passable. But having said that, to be fair, it wouldn't be the sort of place that you would want to send an ambulance, if you could avoid it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Immediately after Grbavica was captured, could you just help me to see whether you recollect the fact that on the 8th of September, in the morning, a group of the civilian police started working, touring houses and making a record of what they found after the capture? Did you come across them? They examined the situation to establish the state of affairs after the military had captured it, to establish what supplies there were, et cetera. In their report, they say that they had a meeting with you after having examined the first three houses. Does this remind you of this?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm fully aware of this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They go on to say that you opposed at the time their continuing their work, but when they came the next day, after quite a bit of talking, it was agreed that a joint group, a mixed group, should do the checking, and the group again consisted of the same civilian police members of the HVO, but there were your men in it, and together they toured a number of buildings and established what they thought were interesting facts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We can agree that even though the locality was not under the control of the military police during that night, nor under any other organised force, nevertheless even the next day some weapons and ammunition were found and that military positions were evident, such as trenches, defence positions, sniper nests, et cetera; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So some weapons and ammunition were not found?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were, sir, only to the same extent as you would expect to find in any Croat or Muslim or Serbian residence. There was one or two -- there was one house that had several arms in that, and if you wish, I can explain the situation that led to the discovery of those weapons. That would probably clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I don't have a translation of this document because I was able to locate it only during the weekend. Of course, I would be happy to provide a translation consequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, does it assist us at all, Mr. Kovacic? Does it take the case any further forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think, yes, it is only for the practical reasons it would be good to have it with the same evidence which were introduced with one witness, but of course it could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste any more time. Have it put on the ELMO, please, and we'll see what it says. Could the usher put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really have no further questions in connection with this. All the questions in this regard have already been put. The document is regrettably only in the Croat language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we get it so we can see the top? What is it supposed to be, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report. It has a number and it has a date, the 10th of September, and one can see from the heading that this is the HVO of Vitez. The signature on the third page shows that the document was signed by the commander of the uniform police, a certain Kresimir Garic. The stamp shows that this is the police station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what I suggest we do is that you get it translated, and then in due course you can apply to have it put it in as an exhibit when it is translated. Thank you. That's all, as far as the exhibit is concerned. Have you much more for this witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure I could be finished before 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Whitworth, we saw quite a few photographs, and you said that you took quite a few of them as well. Let's be quite clear on this. Cerkez is not on a single one of these photographs; right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm assuming that we've changed and you didn't want an explanation to your earlier question about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wouldn't go back for the moment. If Mr. Nice wants to ask you any questions about it, he can do so.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: All right, Sir. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you answer the question related to the photographs? Mr. Mario Cerkez is not on a single one of the photographs shown today; right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Also today we saw quite a few documents, milinfosums. Not in a single one of these documents is Mario Cerkez mentioned, except for one place where you mention the names of the commanders of all the units. But he's not mentioned in any descriptions of events; right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not in the ones that we've seen, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What does "no" mean, that you do mention him somewhere in your reports?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He's mentioned in some milinfo reports, none of which we've seen today. This is only a very brief number of milinfo reports. They were produced normally once, sometimes twice a day, based on whatever was taking place and the level of activity, and it was -- the material was condensed down because it was for publication and telexed throughout the Central Bosnian area, so details about local commanders was often omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whitworth, please, in respect of convoys, we have quite a bit of material given here in the milinfosum 1043. While you were preparing this testimony, did you see the report of the ECMM in relation to the detention of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I haven't, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In any of the reports that concern the convoy, did you see Cerkez's name mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Sorry. In the ones that we actually wrote?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [In English] Correct.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now Z1087, you had it in front of you. I don't think it's been removed. That is milinfosum number 052. It is Z1087. I don't know which page this was, but I think it's the last page. You give a survey of persons, contacts, and units. As for the Vitezovi, you mentioned the Vitezovi as a special unit, and in the footnote you said that it's known to exist but no further details known as yet. But today you said that you knew that Darko Kraljevic was commander of this unit, so wouldn't it be natural to mention here that you knew Darko Kraljevic, Colonel Darko Kraljevic? I mean, what is the reason why no names are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Throughout the tour, we were building a detailed picture of the military and civilian structure. It wasn't very forthcoming from either of the adversaries, and so it took time. This particular milinfo is dated the 20th of June, which is relatively early on. At this particular time, I had had no formal dealings with an organisation of the Vitezovi, though we were aware of their existence because we had seen a badge detailing an organisation of such. I can't remember whether this, date-wise, was before or after the convoy that was trapped in the centre of Vitez, but it was only later that I came to meet, formally, Darko Kraljevic, and he introduced himself as the commander of the Vitezovi to me. That information was not available at this particular time. We weren't in the habit of going up and asking brigade commanders for detailed pictures of their commanders and military structure. We were only interested in that from the point of view of facilitating our U.N. mission. So this was over a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So the core of the matter was that at that point you still did not have a clear picture with regard to the relevant data that you otherwise entered in such documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We added details as we found them, and then we confirmed them in later reports via other source material and again republished it and corrected it as we updated each particular order of OrBat and military organisation. As I say, it wasn't information easily come by, and we were constantly updating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the other footnote on that same page related to the Viteska Brigade. That confirms what you just explained to us. You needed quite a bit of time before you received information, then checked it out, and then only when you were sure, you would enter what you entered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To the best of our ability, that's what we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So on this basis, I can conclude that not later than the 20th of June, you knew for sure that the Viteska Brigade was a completely separate new brigade in relation to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade that previously existed in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir. We had been aware of the existence of the Vitez Brigade effectively since our arrival. Its development had been passed on to us from our predecessors, the Cheshires, and this is just one of the occasions when the intelligence officer sought to keep everybody informed as to what the likes of ourselves and the Colonel would have known on a daily basis, but it generally wasn't known to the rest of the soldiers, so that people could help in building and clarifying the picture as we went along. As to the time scale over which these type of things were published, it varied on the input of information, when we were able to confirm such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. This concerns the unfortunate death of your translator, Dobrila. I have only one question. When this investigations commission was appointed, only one of the investigators who was appointed was from the brigade; is that right? Not the commission, only one person; is that right? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm not quite -- one person from Vitez Brigade? I can recall there was a representative from the Vitez Brigade. If I remember correctly, there were three, maybe four people involved in the commission and myself, and notably no member representing the ABiH. That's my only recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify the situation. Only one person from the brigade, regardless of the capacity in which this person was there? It wasn't the entire group?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall it being as so, but neither can I recall it not being as so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then finally you said, and you explained why, that you could not have agreed with that report. Did you yourself learn some other facts, except for the assessment that you gave us, that showed to you that the conclusion of the commission on the infiltration of the ABiH soldiers was impossible, or was this just the result of your analysis, what you told us, that is?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My analysis, and that of the BritBat military policemen, was that the firing point was quite clearly on the HVO territory. My frustration was with the fact that the HVO representatives in the commission denied any possibility whatsoever that it could have been a Croat or HVO soldier responsible for it, and as far as they were concerned, their only explanation was that it must have been a BiH soldier responsible who had moved across no man's land, taken a shot, and moved back. Our frustration was that we were just intent on bringing somebody to justice. From whichever side that came was irrelevant. We wanted somebody to be held responsible for it so it didn't happen -- to prevent it happening again. In the absence of any other evidence, and in the presence of the supporting ballistic evidence, it was quite clearly identified from an HVO firing point, and yet there was an utter denial by the HVO commission that any Croat or HVO soldier could have been responsible. There was not even a subsequent inquiry to find out if it was possible that somebody could have been involved. Even though we accepted that there was a small arms exchange and that in all likelihood it had happened by accident, we wanted to bring it to people's attention that that was a U.N. building that had been effectively engaged by both sides and caused the death of a U.N. representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You explained this to us once again now, but did you ever receive any documents? Did you ever receive any reliable statements from someone to that effect, that the shooting came from the HVO side? I agree with the analysis, but it's an analysis, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is, based on first-hand experience and knowledge on the ground. There was a formal report made by the commission that was waved in front of me by Darko Gelic, the liaison officer to whom I think the report was submitted, i.e., to Blaskic, and I said I was unhappy with the conclusion of the commission, as to their explanation, because they denied any possibility that it could have been anybody else other than the BiH, despite the fact that I reiterated to them that we were not interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. A brief question. When you discovered that the BH army had manipulated you, that is to say, that you were bringing military equipment unwittingly into Stari Vitez together with medical supplies, until then there had been a few visits already; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was one of only one or two visits that I made that brought medical supplies, and the number and quantity of medical supplies that I personally brought in was very insignificant and would have only facilitated the moving of small arms ammunition. But there were other movements in and out by the ICRC on an infrequent, irregular basis. I couldn't give you the time scale of that. But as I think I said earlier, we employed liaison officers with the ICRC and the UNHCR to employ --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Of course. For you personally, you said this was your first or second time, but then UNPROFOR or, rather, your unit had been there several times to bring in medical supplies; right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a figure, and it was always with my knowledge and permission that they were allowed into the area, so I could keep a rough handle on what was happening in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just confirm the following; it hasn't ever been said quite clearly. Darko Gelic, whom you mentioned a few times, was liaison officer in relation to Colonel Blaskic, from Colonel Blaskic's side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You talked to us quite a bit about communications and equipment. Tell me, please, since you are a specialist in this area and since you had the relevant knowledge with the communications equipment that the BH army had, and you already mentioned it, could they listen to the radio communications of HVO units, in your opinion, on the basis of what you knew they had? Just talking about Stari Vitez. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The types of radios I saw being used by the ABiH in Stari Vitez, it wouldn't have been possible to listen in to the HVO unless they had the identical same handset, and, even in that case, it required the same frequency fill in order for it to do that. If, on the other hand, they had military-type radios which are simply a frequency-tuning device, as we found they tuned into ours, they would have been able to listen to ours as well as the HVO if they were using VHF or HF communications. But I didn't see any evidence of that in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: VHF?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Very high frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Not to waste any time, we saw a picture here where a BH army soldier held a "baby." We know what we are talking about, don't we? Is this a "baby" that was made by the BH side, or was it manufactured by the HVO side, that is to say, this particular example that we saw?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was one that had been fired into Stari Vitez and had not gone off. The fuse had obviously been damaged. You can see the damage occurred to it as it had fallen. But they were home-made, improvised devices and therefore not 100 per cent reliable. But that one was manufactured by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you hear about the Muslim side in the conflict manufacturing this same device? It was actually their invention which the HVO had later taken over. Did you have the opportunity of hearing that or seeing that they had a similar weapon?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I could well believe that's true, but I have no knowledge or experience of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You mentioned that little anecdote was in connection to Cerkez and Radio Vitez in the sense of propaganda. Please, isn't it customary in any conflict for the parties involved in the conflict to use propaganda?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did both sides resort to propaganda in this conflict as well?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Because of the nature of the geographical area I was working in, I am not familiar with any ABiH form of propaganda as such, but I don't doubt that it took place on a similar basis. Under the -- because of poor communications, rumours were rife and in great abundance, and it was quite easy to spread such propaganda by word of mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You said at one point that it was difficult at times to distinguish between the regular and irregular units. Could you please tell me whether it was easier, perhaps, to distinguish between regular units? I mean, according to insignia, weapons, whatever, could you distinguish between different regular units of the HVO? Did you know exactly which ones were which?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It's not always easy to clearly define membership to one unit or another. It depends whether they're wearing any insignia. Unless they were wearing insignia, then we took them to be members of the local geographic militia of that particular area. Those who wore insignia tended to wear it with pride and were usually part of the specialist units. Those were the one that we usually saw worn. Although the HVO militia badge was very commonplace, it wasn't in ample supply so everybody had one, and people obviously -- not everybody was equipped with uniforms. So the short answer would be no, it's not always easy to identify which unit people are affiliated to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can we say, generally speaking, that these special units -- for example, the Jokeri, the Vitezovi, the Tvrtko units -- were well-armed in terms of the quality and quantity of the weapons they had, as compared to the Viteska Brigade that was poorly armed with dated weapons, et cetera? Would that be a way of making a distinction between them?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wouldn't have said the Vitez Brigade were poorly armed with dated weapons. They had modern weapon systems amongst them, but yes, the general rule would be that the specialist units would be better equipped and have a more ample supply of more modern, up-to-date weapons, handguns, automatic machine guns, that type of thing. And examples the likes of which you saw with the sniper rifle; that wouldn't -- it's not the sort of thing that would be found in the Vitez Brigade armoury, as it were, or I wouldn't have thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Karlo Grabovac, whom you mentioned as the local commander of the HVO in the territory of Rijeka, that is to say, a member of the brigade, you said that you knew him relatively well and that you had a lot of meetings with him. Would you agree if I say that he was relatively cooperative in his relationship with you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Karlo and I got to know each other very, very well. He was well-liked and respected by the people in his brigade area, and he had a good rapport and relationship with commander Cerkez, and for the most part he was very pleasant and affable. But as far as co-operation was concerned, that was very dependent on what I was trying to achieve at the end of the day. For example, if I wanted to move an aid convoy through to Kruscica, then the answer would be a firm but polite no. As I say, we had several meetings; we got on very well. We drank coffee and Slivovitz together, and I made every effort to get on well with the chap in order to facilitate my movement through the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, will we agree if I say that he never cheated, that he would never promise you one thing and do another thing? I meant fair-minded in that sense; he was also building a relationship, as you were. Right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was building a relationship; I think that's correct. I can't recall any such instance, in which he said one thing and did another. If he'd been told by commander Cerkez that my movement wasn't to be allowed in a particular area, then he would be polite, but would deny my access as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point you said that the HVO was in a way afraid of Kraljevic, if that's the right word; that they had some reservations vis-a-vis Kraljevic. What about the civilians in Vitez? Did they share that feeling? Is that the picture you had?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To a certain degree, yes. He was seen as a very effective military commander and a local hero as far as the people of Vitez were concerned. But my impression was that he was also a very volatile and unpredictable character, a little bit unstable in some respects, and that the people I spoke to about him were aware of that volatility and that element of unpredictability. But he was still held in high regard as one of the key figures in the Lasva Valley area responsible for their continued safe existence in the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You said that it seemed that Cerkez and Kraljevic had relatively good relations, but that you saw them together only once, and that you heard on a few occasions that they were somewhere together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct. So there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was just -- there were two or three occasions when I went to visit commander Cerkez, and I was told by his officers in the cinema building that he was out on the grounds somewhere and unavailable to speak to me. Then I would visit the commanders adjacent to him, and Kraljevic was one of those in the Gornji Vecerska area, and when visiting his headquarters in Gornji Vecerska, there were a couple of occasions when Kraljevic wasn't present, and it was told to me by the people present that he was up country, planning a military activity, and that Cerkez's name was involved alongside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Stari Vitez --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it is 4.00. How much longer are you going to be now, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I actually have another short topic with perhaps two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Stari Vitez, we know where it is situated geographically, a narrow valley surrounded by heights to the north and the south. Generally speaking, this whole area of Vitez, the town itself and Stari Vitez, are actually surrounded by BH army units that were holding certain positions, strongholds, overlooking the valley, both to the north and the south; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. The HVO were at a geographical and tactical disadvantage because of the nature of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it true, in military terms, is it strategically normal for the BH army to try and cut across the valley, at least at one point, and later on in the war that was its aim? Did you come to the same conclusion, as an observer and an analyst of the situation?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong: You are saying that it would be advantageous to the BiH to sever the main road across the valley, cut across the valley and sever the main road and the link between Vitez and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My question is whether, at any stage during the war, that was one of the aims of the BH army, to sever the valley, to cut across the valley.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the specific aims of the ABiH, but from my analysis and from our analysis, it would go a long way to breaking the resolve of the HVO forces in the Lasva Valley if they were then isolated into pockets of Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik. But our suspicions were that the ABiH weren't fully committed to such a military operation, and that from their tactical advantage on the hills, they were effectively doing something very similar without committing a considerable amount of military resources to doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And my final question. Can we agree, without going into the details, but generally speaking, that the situation, as time went on through the summer and the autumn, that the situation worsened for the HVO, that the ABiH was gaining in strength and the HVO was losing? Generally speaking, would that be a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think the HVO and the likes of commander Cerkez and Blaskic were put under increasing pressure because of various ABiH military successes; for example, the fall of Travnik. Obviously their ability to sustain themselves was under threat because of the increasing number of people in an ever decreasingly small area. So yes, they were under a considerable amount of duress and pressure towards the latter half of the tour, of our period of time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whitworth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, a few questions for monosyllabic answers if you can. Did the HVO offer for Stari Vitez residents to leave with any guarantees to them of return to their property, preservation of property, or any such guarantees?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, it came with no such guarantee, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke of Kordic being present at the Convoy of Joy at some stage. We may have heard about this from elsewhere, but to identify the time when you saw him, what, if anything, was he doing? In a word, or at most, a sentence.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't -- I couldn't -- I could only say that he was present, and not actually -- I can't recall him actually doing anything other than being --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. That's all. Milinfosum number 43, please; can you have it in front of you? Two questions about the form of these documents. Paragraph 3, "Comment" is underlined. Before that we have a reference to Kordic being a power, and so on; after that we have a conclusion. Is the format that the material coming before "Comment" is raw material from people on the ground, and that "Comment" is the analysis of the intelligence officer that follows the word "Comment"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the bit before "Comment," in all likelihood, is from me, because I had regular dialogues with Karlo. The bit afterwards is the intelligence officer's assimilation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second-to-last page on the same document, again, a question of form. If we look up to the second-to-the-last paragraph, for example, where there is a reference to direct personal orders of Dario Kordic, was that a conclusion, or was that information being presented to the intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Sorry, can you elaborate on which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second-to-last page, part of the Convoy of Joy summary, second-to-last or third-to-last paragraph, the bit that refers to direct orders of Dario Kordic. Is that analysis or is that intelligence?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That would have been intelligence, based on comments on the ground, and in all likelihood, was based in part on the comment I made in the general report at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the front page, the last question on this document, at the end of paragraph 3, there is reference to human barricades being contrived. Did that fit with, or not, your own observation?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, it did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the HVO have HIP or any type of helicopters, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They used them -- they organised and used them for the casualty evacuations from Kiseljak, so they had -- if they didn't have them, they had access to them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did they actually own any or have any of their own?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the HVO in Vitez having their own access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the specialist groups, your own military experience, just this question. If specialist groups were working in an area like Vitez, would it, in your judgement, be with -- even if they weren't directly seconded to the local brigade commander, would it be with the knowledge of or/and co-operation of the local commander?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It would have to be, to ensure any success, or else there would be major organisational problems and a potential blue on blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: People kept in Cerkez's cellar before exchange, were you aware of the conditions, physical or psychological, of any one of those particular people?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: One of them, the one of whom I have a recollection had a chronic illness, something like TB or something like that, was in poor health but was not kept in an adequate medical facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I should object. The witness never said "Cerkez's cellar."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was Mr. Nice who claimed that, but I don't think it was supported by the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other point on Cerkez and his position. You've been asked about brigades and brigadiers. Is it sensible to match Cerkez's position with a conventional rank or not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was a brigade commander in their terms, and as I said earlier, he had a similar rank, but he -- so we assumed he was a brigade commander. But that is always subordinate to Colonel Blaskic, who was effectively a divisional commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that in conventional terms, Blaskic would have held a senior rank to the rank he actually held?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document -- no, perhaps just this. You wanted to add something about the joint civil and criminal groups' finding of weapons; you wanted to explain how they found weapons. In a sentence, if it's significant, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: On the particular night, the attack on Grbavica, the assault by the HVO was mounted from the barracks side of Grbavica, so they used our barracks as a launch point for the assaults. The houses immediately outside the barracks were actually occupied by the likes of myself and the other liaison officers and were actually Muslim-owned houses that we were renting. That particular night, as we've previously stated on numerous occasions, a lot of the local people held arms, and because of the nature of the assault, all the local Muslims who did a lot of chores around the camp and who lived in the houses outside took shelter in one particular house. They had with them their own personal firearms. There were a couple of local civilians shot and killed in my house personally, and in order to try and defuse the situation, I arranged for their movement to Travnik, to a Muslim area, told them to leave all the weapons where they were, but they claimed they were under the protection of the U.N. because they were actually in U.N.-rented accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was those weapons that were found?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: And it was those weapons that were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO report, for which we will in due course have a translation, were you aware of that being prepared at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No. I wasn't familiar with the policeman who is a respectable character, and he was quite affable when I informed him of the situation and that we were -- what I was planning to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That remains only, then, the one exhibit, Your Honour, that I said I would produce. I distributed it just after lunch, I think. May the witness produce the milinfosum for the 15th of September? It will be Z1201,2. Does the witness have it before him? Maybe not. He's the one person who hasn't got it. It's coming. I think the Defence have had it. Under "Vitez," it refers to the HVO issuing the ultimatum to the Muslims in Stari Vitez to leave the area or face the consequences. And in the comment that follows the raw material: "Although less fiercer than their earlier attack on Grbavica, this HVO attack has again met with little response by the BiH. It is becoming apparent that despite Alagic's recent claims, there has still not been any effective BiH counterattack on the Croat pocket. Indeed, the HVO are capitalising on their recent success and continuing to push forward. The reasons for this are many and varied, but it is possible that at present the BiH in the Lasva Valley are more heavily committed elsewhere than originally assessed." Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming again to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I could have two or three minutes' private session with the Chamber, I would be grateful. If it's straining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two minutes, two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of October, 1999, at 9.30 a.m.
